topics.goal: A narrow pulse has a wide spectrum; this is the uncertainty principle before quantum mechanics.
checks: I can explain why a narrow signal must have a wide spectrum.

ex.q: A Gaussian has width σ in x. What is its width in k, and what is their product?
ex.a: 1/(2σ) in k as a standard deviation; product 1/2

ex.q: A beep lasts 1 ms. Roughly how spread out are its frequencies?
Multiply by ħ using p = ħk. Which famous inequality appears?
Why can a radar not measure a target's distance and speed perfectly with a single pulse?
ex.a: A short pulse pins down distance but blurs frequency, and speed comes from the frequency shift.

topics.title: Convolution
topics.goal: Convolution and the convolution theorem.
checks: I can convolve two distributions and use the convolution theorem.

ex.q: Convolve the distributions of two dice. What is P(sum = 7)?
Convolve a box with itself. What shape appears?
Multiply (1 + 2x)(3 + x) by convolving coefficient lists.
Explain blurring a photo as a convolution and as a product of Fourier transforms.

topics.title: The Dirac delta
topics.goal: Use δ(x) as an infinitely sharp spike with area 1.
checks: I can integrate against δ(x) and see it as a limit of narrow peaks.

ex.q: Integrate δ(x − 2) x² over all x.
Show δ(2x) = ½δ(x).
Show that Gaussians of width σ and area 1 behave like δ(x) as σ → 0.
What is the derivative of the step function?
Use 5.13 Exercise 4 to argue that the integral of e^(ikx) over all k is 2πδ(x).

topics.title: Parseval's theorem
topics.goal: Energy is the same in position and frequency space.
checks: I can state Parseval's theorem and use it to sum a series.

ex.q: Apply Parseval to the square wave to find 1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + …
In quantum terms, what does Parseval say about total probability in position and momentum space?
ex.a: It is the same in both.

topics.title: The Laplace transform
topics.goal: Turn ODEs into algebra.
checks: I can transform simple functions and solve an ODE with them.

ex.q: Transform 1, e^(at) and sin ωt.
Solve y′ + y = 0 with y(0) = 1.
Solve y″ + y = 0 with y(0) = 0 and y′(0) = 1.

topics.title: Calculus of variations
topics.search: calculus of variations Euler-Lagrange equation brachistochrone
topics.goal: Find the path that minimizes an integral (the gateway to least action).
checks: I can derive and apply the Euler-Lagrange equation.

ex.q: Derive the Euler-Lagrange equation for minimizing the integral of F(y, y′, x).
Show that the shortest path between two points is a straight line.
A soap film between two rings takes the shape of least area. Show the profile is y = a cosh(x/a) (see 2.26).
What curve gives the fastest slide under gravity (the brachistochrone)?

topics.title: Sturm-Liouville theory
topics.goal: Why eigenfunctions of physical operators are orthogonal and complete.
checks: I can explain why eigenfunctions of these operators are orthogonal.

ex.q: Show y″ + λy = 0 is a Sturm-Liouville problem.
Prove that two eigenfunctions with different λ are orthogonal, using integration by parts.
Write Legendre's equation (1 − x²)y″ − 2xy′ + l(l + 1)y = 0 in Sturm-Liouville form.

topics.title: Orthogonal polynomials
topics.goal: Polynomials as orthogonal basis vectors.
checks: I can expand a function in an orthogonal polynomial basis.

ex.q: Check that x and (3x² − 1)/2 are orthogonal on [−1, 1].
Write x² as a combination of P₀ = 1 and P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2.
Which weight functions go with Hermite and Laguerre polynomials?

topics.title: Legendre polynomials
topics.goal: Angular solutions in spherical problems.
checks: I can generate P₀ to P₃ and say where they appear.

ex.q: Generate P₀ to P₃ with Rodrigues' formula Pₙ = (1/(2ⁿ n!)) dⁿ/dxⁿ (x² − 1)ⁿ.
Check that Pₙ(1) = 1 for each.
1/|r − r′| expands in powers of r′/r with Pₙ(cos θ) as coefficients. Which physics idea does this give? (See 11.30.)

topics.title: Spherical harmonics
topics.goal: The shapes of atomic orbitals come from these.
checks: I can link the Y_l^m to atomic orbital shapes.

ex.q: Check that Y₀⁰ = 1/√(4π) is normalized over the sphere.
Y₁⁰ is proportional to cos θ. Describe its shape. Which orbital is it?
ex.a: Two lobes along z: the p_z orbital

ex.q: How many Y_l^m are there for l = 2? Which orbitals are they?

topics.title: Hermite polynomials
topics.goal: The quantum oscillator's wavefunctions.
checks: I can build the harmonic oscillator wavefunctions from Hermite polynomials.

ex.q: Write H₀, H₁ and H₂.
Show ψ = x e^(−x²/2) satisfies −ψ″ + x²ψ = 3ψ. (This is the first excited oscillator state, in units where E = 2n + 1.)
Check that H₀ and H₂ are orthogonal with weight e^(−x²).

topics.title: Laguerre polynomials
topics.goal: The radial part of hydrogen wavefunctions.
checks: I can say where Laguerre polynomials appear in hydrogen.

ex.q: Write L₀, L₁ and L₂.
The hydrogen 2s radial function is (2 − r/a) e^(−r/2a). Where is its node?

topics.title: Bessel functions
topics.goal: Cylindrical waves and drumheads.
checks: I can describe J₀ and why drums sound different from strings.

ex.q: Sketch J₀(x) and mark its first two zeros (2.405 and 5.520).
A drum's lowest modes have frequencies in the ratio of Bessel zeros. Why doesn't a drum sound a clean musical note like a string?
ex.a: 5.520/2.405 ≈ 2.30 and the other modes are not whole-number multiples, so overtones clash.

topics.title: The gamma function
topics.goal: Factorials for non-integers.
checks: I can use Γ(n) = (n − 1)! and compute Γ(1/2).

ex.q: Show Γ(n + 1) = nΓ(n) with integration by parts.
Show Γ(1/2) = √π using the Gaussian integral.
What is (1/2)!?
The volume of an n-dimensional ball is π^(n/2) Rⁿ/Γ(n/2 + 1). Check it for n = 2 and n = 3.

topics.title: Green's functions
topics.goal: Solve a PDE once for a point source, then add up (the idea behind propagators).
checks: I can explain a Green's function as the response to a point kick.

ex.q: Find the Green's function of d²/dx² on [0, 1] with zero ends.
ex.a: G = x(s − 1) for x < s and s(x − 1) for x > s

ex.q: The Green's function of ∇² in 3D is −1/(4πr). How does superposition then give the potential of any charge distribution?
ex.a: Add up −1/(4πr) responses from every bit of charge

ex.q: Describe the response of a resting oscillator to a sudden hammer blow.
ex.a: It rings as a decaying sine.

topics.title: Complex differentiability
topics.search: complex analysis introduction holomorphic functions Cauchy-Riemann
topics.goal: What differentiable means for complex functions.
checks: I can test the Cauchy-Riemann equations.

ex.q: Check that z² satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann equations.
ex.a: u = x² − y² and v = 2xy give u_x = v_y = 2x and u_y = −v_x = −2y

ex.q: Is the conjugate z̄ complex-differentiable?
Show that the real and imaginary parts of z² each solve Laplace's equation.

topics.title: Contour integration and residues
topics.goal: Evaluate hard real integrals using complex poles.
checks: I can evaluate real integrals with the residue theorem.

ex.q: Integrate 1/z around the unit circle.
Use the residue at i to integrate 1/(1 + x²) over the real line. Compare with 2.21.
Integrate 1/(1 + x⁴) over the real line.
Find the residue of e^z/z³ at 0.

topics.title: The zeta function and analytic continuation
topics.goal: How 1 + 2 + 3 + … gets assigned −1/12 (it shows up in the Casimir effect and string theory).
checks: I can explain what "1 + 2 + 3 + … = −1/12" really means.

ex.q: Add 1/n² for n up to 1000 in code and compare with π²/6.
In two sentences, explain why ζ(−1) = −1/12 is not the sum of 1 + 2 + 3 + …
ex.a: The sum diverges; −1/12 is the value of a smooth continuation of ζ to a point where the series makes no sense.

topics.title: Conformal maps
topics.goal: Angle-preserving maps.
checks: I can describe how a complex function bends a grid while keeping angles.

ex.q: What does z ↦ z² do to horizontal and vertical grid lines?
ex.a: Hyperbolas (and parabolas from lines away from the axes)

ex.q: Show that z ↦ z + 1/z sends the unit circle to a line segment. Which segment?

topics.title: Numerical ODE solving
topics.goal: Simulate an ODE on a computer.
checks: I can implement Euler's method and RK4.

ex.q: Use Euler's method on y′ = y, y(0) = 1, to t = 1 with step 0.1. Compare with e.
Repeat with RK4. How big is the error now?
Simulate a pendulum with RK4 and plot θ(t) for a small and a large swing.

topics.title: Solving the Schrödinger equation numerically
topics.search: solve Schrodinger equation numerically Python finite difference
topics.goal: Turn a PDE into a matrix eigenvalue problem and solve it.
checks: I can turn −½ψ″ + Vψ = Eψ into a matrix and find its eigenvalues.

ex.q: Discretize −½ψ″ = Eψ on [0, 1] with ψ = 0 at both ends using 100 grid points, and find the lowest eigenvalues with numpy. Compare with n²π²/2.
Add V = 50(x − 0.5)² and plot the ground state.
Build a double well and look at the two lowest states. What do you notice about their energies? (This is tunneling splitting, see 23.9b.)
ex.a: The two lowest are nearly equal; the tiny gap is set by tunneling through the barrier.

topics.title: The logistic map
topics.goal: How simple equations produce chaos.
checks: I can explain period doubling and chaos.

ex.q: Iterate x → rx(1 − x) from 0.2 with r = 2.5. Where does it settle?
Repeat with r = 3.2.
Repeat with r = 3.9 for two starting points 0.2 and 0.2001.
ex.a: The two runs separate completely within a few dozen steps

ex.q: Period doubling happens near r = 3, 3.449 and 3.544. Estimate the Feigenbaum ratio from these.

topics.title: The Lorenz attractor
topics.goal: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions.
checks: I can explain sensitive dependence on initial conditions.

ex.q: Simulate the Lorenz system with σ = 10, ρ = 28, β = 8/3 and plot it in 3D.
Start two runs 10⁻⁸ apart. Plot their distance over time on a log scale.
ex.a: The distance grows exponentially until it is the size of the attractor

ex.q: What does this mean for weather forecasts?

topics.title: Perturbation methods
topics.goal: Approximate when a parameter is small.
checks: I can solve a problem as a series in a small parameter.

ex.q: Solve x² + εx − 1 = 0 for the positive root to first order in ε, then check against the exact formula.
Stirling's formula says ln n! ≈ n ln n − n + ½ ln(2πn). Test it at n = 10.
Why can a series that diverges still give excellent approximations if you stop early?
ex.a: The first terms shrink before they grow.

parts.name: Probability
parts.title: Probability, statistics and information
parts.intro: Quantum mechanics only ever predicts probabilities; here you learn to compute them, spread them and test them, and you estimate how long sunlight takes to escape the Sun.

topics.title: Probability basics
topics.goal: Probability from 0 to 1; adding for "or", multiplying for "and".
checks: I can add probabilities for "or" and multiply them for independent "and".

ex.q: What is the chance of rolling a 6? Of not rolling a 6?
Roll two dice. What is the chance both show 6? That at least one shows 6?
Draw one card. What is the chance it is a heart or a king?
Birthday problem: with 23 people in a room, what is the chance two share a birthday? (Compute the chance that all differ first.)
A fair coin has landed heads 10 times in a row. What is the chance of heads next?

topics.title: Conditional probability
topics.goal: Compute P(A given B).
checks: I can compute P(A given B) and avoid the classic traps.

ex.q: A family has two children and at least one is a boy. What is the chance both are boys?
Draw two cards without replacement. What is the chance both are aces?
The first die shows 3. What is the chance the two dice sum to 8?
Monty Hall: you pick one of three doors, the host opens an empty one of the other two. Should you switch? Prove it.
ex.a: Yes: switching wins 2/3 of the time.

topics.title: Bayes' theorem
topics.goal: Update beliefs with evidence.
checks: I can update a probability with new evidence using Bayes' theorem.

ex.q: 1% of people have a disease. A test catches 90% of cases but gives a false positive to 9% of healthy people. You test positive. What is the chance you are sick?
You take the test again and are positive again. Update your answer.
Explain in a sentence why a rare condition makes a single positive test weak evidence.
ex.a: Most positives come from the large healthy group.

topics.title: Expected value
topics.goal: Compute an average outcome (expectation values later).
checks: I can compute expected values and use linearity.

ex.q: Find the expected roll of one die.
A bet wins 10 € with probability 0.1 and loses 1 € otherwise. Is it worth taking?
Find the expected value of the square of a die roll.
Find the expected sum of two dice without listing outcomes.
A spin measurement gives +1 with probability 0.75 and −1 with probability 0.25. What is the average result? (This is a quantum expectation value.)

topics.title: Variance and standard deviation
topics.goal: Measure spread. The Δx in the uncertainty principle is a standard deviation.
checks: I can compute variance and standard deviation and know how they scale.

ex.q: Find the variance and standard deviation of a die roll (use 6.4 Exercise 3).
Find the mean and standard deviation of 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9.
Show Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X).
Find the standard deviation of the spin measurement in 6.4 Exercise 5.
In the uncertainty principle, Δx is a standard deviation. Of what, exactly? Explain in terms of many repeated experiments.
ex.a: The spread of results over many identically prepared systems.

topics.title: Probability densities
topics.goal: Probability as area under a density curve; ∣ψ∣² is a density.
checks: I can find probabilities, means and normalization from a density.

ex.q: X is uniform on [0, 2]. What is its density, and P(0.5 < X < 1)?
Check that p(x) = 3x² on [0, 1] is normalized and find its mean.
A particle in a box of length 1 has density 2 sin²(πx). What is the chance of finding it in the left quarter of the box?
A nucleus decays at a random time with density λe^(−λt). What is its average lifetime?

topics.title: The binomial distribution
topics.goal: Count successes in repeated trials.
checks: I can compute binomial probabilities, mean and spread.

ex.q: What is the chance of exactly 3 heads in 5 tosses?
Derive the mean np of the binomial distribution using linearity.
100 photons each have a 0.6 chance of being detected. Find the mean count and its standard deviation.
You measure 1000 identical qubits that each give 1 with probability 0.3. How many 1s do you expect, give or take?

topics.title: The Poisson distribution
topics.goal: Count rare events (photon detections, radioactive decays).
checks: I can use P(k) = λᵏ e^(−λ)/k! for counts of rare events.

ex.q: A Geiger counter averages 3 clicks per second. What is the chance of 0 clicks in a second? Of exactly 3?
For a Poisson count, the variance equals the mean. What is the relative noise on a count of 100? Of 10,000?
A faint star gives 100 photons per exposure. How many photons would you need for 1% precision?
Look up Bortkiewicz's data on Prussian cavalry deaths from horse kicks. Why is it a famous Poisson example?
ex.a: Rare independent events fit Poisson closely.

topics.title: The normal distribution
topics.goal: Use mean and σ of a Gaussian.
checks: I know the 68-95-99.7 rule and can convert to standard scores.

ex.q: Heights have mean 175 cm and standard deviation 7 cm. What fraction of people are taller than 189 cm?
What is the standard score of a 161 cm person?
The oscillator ground state has ψ ∝ e^(−x²/2), so |ψ|² ∝ e^(−x²). What is the standard deviation of the position?

topics.title: The central limit theorem
topics.goal: Why Gaussians appear everywhere.
checks: I can explain why averages of many random things look Gaussian.

ex.q: In code, plot histograms of the average of 1, 2 and 10 dice over 100,000 trials.
You average 100 die rolls. What are the mean and standard deviation of that average?
Why are measurement errors often Gaussian, even when no single error source is?
ex.a: Many small independent errors add up.

topics.title: Joint distributions and correlation
topics.goal: Tell correlation from independence (key for Bell tests).
checks: I can compute covariance and correlation and tell correlation from independence.

ex.q: Two independent dice: what is the covariance of their values?
X is a die roll and Y = 7 − X. What is their correlation?
Give an example of two strongly correlated quantities where neither causes the other.
ex.a: Ice cream sales and sunburn (both caused by sunny days).

ex.q: Two coins always land opposite. Explain how pre-arranged instructions could cause this. Bell's theorem (15.26) shows quantum correlations cannot always be explained that way.

topics.title: Random walks and diffusion
topics.goal: A random walk spreads as √t.
checks: I can explain why a random walk spreads as √(number of steps).

ex.q: After 100 random steps of ±1, about how far are you from the start?
Simulate 1000 such walkers in code and check your answer.
Sugar spreads 1 cm in tea in a minute. About how long to spread 2 cm?
A photon in the Sun travels about 1 mm before being scattered in a random direction. The Sun's radius is 7 × 10⁸ m. Estimate the number of steps to escape, then the time. (Light speed 3 × 10⁸ m/s.)
ex.a: About (7 × 10¹¹)² ≈ 5 × 10²³ steps; about 1.6 × 10¹² s, roughly 50,000 years (published estimates range from 10⁴ to 10⁵ years).

topics.title: Monte Carlo methods
topics.goal: Estimate answers with random sampling.
checks: I can estimate a number by random sampling and know how the error shrinks.

ex.q: Estimate π by throwing random points into a unit square and counting those inside the quarter circle.
The error shrinks as 1/√N. About how many points for 3 correct decimals?
Look up Buffon's needle and estimate π with real matches and floorboards.

topics.title: Bayesian and frequentist probability
topics.goal: What probability means (this matters for QBism in Part 19).
checks: I can explain the two meanings of probability.

ex.q: What does "70% chance of rain tomorrow" mean to a frequentist and to a Bayesian?
ex.a: Frequentist: on days like this it rains 70% of the time. Bayesian: your confidence in rain is 0.7

ex.q: A coin gave 7 heads in 10 tosses. Give the frequentist estimate of p, and the Bayesian average of p starting from a uniform prior (the answer is (heads + 1)/(tosses + 2)).
Is a Born-rule probability a frequency or a degree of belief? Write your view now and compare it with QBism in 19.6.

topics.title: Five sigma
topics.search: five sigma statistical significance particle physics
topics.goal: How discoveries like the Higgs boson are claimed.
checks: I can explain what a 5-sigma discovery claims and what it does not.

ex.q: About how likely is a fluctuation beyond 5σ in one direction by chance?
What is the look-elsewhere effect, and why does it matter when searching many energies?
ex.a: Looking in many places makes a fluke somewhere likely

ex.q: Look up the 750 GeV diphoton excess at the LHC (2015 to 2016). What happened to it?

topics.title: Shannon entropy
topics.goal: Information measured in bits (leads to von Neumann entropy).
checks: I can compute entropy in bits and explain what it measures.

ex.q: Find the entropy of a fair coin and a fair die.
Find the entropy of a coin that lands heads 90% of the time.
Why can a file full of a biased coin's results be compressed?
ex.a: Each result carries less than 1 bit

ex.q: How many yes/no questions does it take to identify one item out of 1,000,000?

topics.title: KL divergence and mutual information
topics.goal: Distance between distributions; shared information.
checks: I can compute KL divergence and explain mutual information.

ex.q: Find the KL divergence from a fair coin to a 90%-heads coin, D(fair ‖ biased), in bits.
Find D(biased ‖ fair). Why is it different?
ex.a: About 0.53 bits; KL divergence is not symmetric

ex.q: What is the mutual information of two coins that always land the same? Of two independent coins?

parts.name: Advanced Math
parts.title: Advanced math for quantum theory
parts.intro: Come back here when Parts 16 and 20 ask for it. Highlight: in 7.11 you show that turning an electron by 360° multiplies its state by −1.

topics.title: Hilbert space
topics.goal: The infinite-dimensional vector space of square-integrable wavefunctions.
checks: I can say which functions are square-integrable and why that matters.

ex.q: Is e^(−x²) square-integrable on ℝ? Is 1/x on [1, ∞)? Is the constant 1 on ℝ?
Is a plane wave e^(ikx) in L²(ℝ)? Why do physicists use it anyway?
ex.a: No, it cannot be normalized; wave packets built from plane waves can

ex.q: Check that ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫ f*(x) g(x) dx satisfies the inner product rules.
Show that √2 sin(nπx), n = 1, 2, 3, …, is an orthonormal set on [0, 1].

topics.title: Functional analysis
topics.goal: Norms, completeness, operators on function spaces.
checks: I can explain norms, completeness and bounded operators.

ex.q: Give a sequence of rationals whose limit is not rational. What does this say about completeness?
ex.a: 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, … tends to √2: ℚ is not complete

ex.q: Find the L² norm of f(x) = x on [0, 1].
Does fₙ(x) = sin(nx)/n tend to 0 in L²[0, π]?
Show that multiplying by sin x is a bounded operator on L²[0, π]. What is its norm?

topics.title: Differential operators as matrices
topics.goal: See d/dx as a linear operator with eigenfunctions.
checks: I can write a derivative on a grid as a matrix.

ex.q: Write the central-difference matrix for d/dx on 5 grid points with spacing h (zero outside).
Write d²/dx² as the tridiagonal matrix with −2 on the diagonal and 1 beside it (divided by h²). How does this connect to 5.34?
ex.a: It is exactly the matrix used there

ex.q: Using integration by parts, show d/dx is anti-Hermitian on functions vanishing at the ends, so −i d/dx is Hermitian.
ex.a: ∫ f* g′ = −∫ f*′ g when the boundary terms vanish.

topics.title: Self-adjoint and unbounded operators
topics.search: bounded and unbounded operators self-adjoint vs Hermitian
topics.goal: Why position and momentum need extra care.
checks: I can explain why position and momentum need care.

ex.q: Show p = −iħ d/dx is symmetric on functions that vanish at ±∞.
On [0, 1] with ψ(0) = ψ(1) = 0, does p have any eigenfunctions? Why is that strange?
ex.a: No: e^(ikx) cannot vanish at both ends, so p has no eigenvectors even though it is symmetric

ex.q: Show ψ with |ψ|² = 1/(π(1 + x²)) is normalized but has infinite ⟨x²⟩.

topics.title: Discrete and continuous spectrum
topics.goal: Bound states vs scattering states.
checks: I can tell bound states from scattering states.

ex.q: For a finite square well, which energies are discrete and which continuous?
ex.a: Bound states below the rim are discrete; above it, continuous

ex.q: For hydrogen, what physical situation do E < 0 and E > 0 describe?
ex.a: A bound electron and an ionized one

ex.q: Why are continuum states normalized with δ-functions instead of to 1?

topics.title: Distributions
topics.goal: Make the delta function rigorous.
checks: I can manipulate δ and its derivatives under integrals.

ex.q: Show ∫ δ′(x) f(x) dx = −f′(0).
Show xδ(x) = 0.
Show δ(x² − a²) = [δ(x − a) + δ(x + a)]/(2|a|).
Differentiate |x| twice in the sense of distributions.

topics.title: Rigged Hilbert space
topics.goal: Why position eigenstates are not true Hilbert space vectors.
checks: I can explain why |x⟩ is not a normalizable state but is still useful.

ex.q: In one paragraph, explain how ⟨x|x′⟩ = δ(x − x′) replaces normalization to 1.
Name the three spaces of a Gelfand triple and which kind of object lives in each.
ex.a: The space of nice test functions, the Hilbert space, and its dual of distributions, where |x⟩ lives.

topics.title: Group theory
topics.goal: Group axioms with rotations and permutations.
checks: I can check the group axioms and tell abelian from non-abelian groups.

ex.q: Is {1, −1, i, −i} a group under multiplication?
List the symmetries of an equilateral triangle. How many are there? Do they commute?
ex.a: Six (3 rotations including identity, 3 reflections); no

ex.q: Are the integers a group under subtraction?
The Rubik's cube group has about 4.3 × 10¹⁹ elements. Why is it non-abelian?
ex.a: Turning two faces in different orders gives different results.

topics.title: Representations
topics.goal: Groups acting as matrices on vector spaces.
checks: I can represent a group by matrices and compute characters.

ex.q: Represent {1, i, −1, −i} by 2 × 2 rotation matrices.
Represent the triangle symmetries by 3 × 3 permutation matrices.
Find the characters (traces) of that representation for each type of symmetry.

topics.title: Lie groups and Lie algebras
topics.search: Lie groups and Lie algebras introduction
topics.goal: Continuous symmetries and their generators.
checks: I can find generators and their commutators.

ex.q: Write the generator of rotations in the plane and exponentiate it (see 3.24).
ex.a: J = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]; e^(θJ) is the rotation by θ

ex.q: Write the 3 × 3 generators Lx, Ly, Lz of 3D rotations and check [Lx, Ly] = Lz.
Rotate a book 90° about x then y, and then in the other order. Why do tiny rotations nearly commute but large ones don't?
ex.a: The commutator is second order in the angles.

topics.title: SO(3), SU(2) and the double cover
topics.goal: Why there are two kinds of rotation behaviour.
checks: I can explain why SU(2) covers SO(3) twice.

ex.q: Compute e^(−iθσz/2) at θ = 2π and θ = 4π.
Do the plate trick (or belt trick). How does it show a 720° loop can be undone but a 360° one cannot?
How many parameters do SU(2) and SO(3) each have?

topics.title: Spinors
topics.goal: Objects that flip sign after a 360° rotation.
checks: I can rotate a spinor and explain the sign flip.

ex.q: Rotate the spinor (1, 0) by 2π about z using 7.11 Exercise 1.
Write spin up along x as a spinor.
A global sign never shows up in probabilities. How can the 360° sign flip be measured? (See 23.27.)
ex.a: By interfering a rotated beam with an unrotated one.

topics.title: Quaternions
topics.goal: Quaternions as 3D rotations (closely related to SU(2)).
checks: I can multiply quaternions and use them to rotate vectors.

ex.q: Using i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1, find ij and ji.
Rotate the vector i by 90° about the z-axis with q = cos 45° + k sin 45° and q i q*.
Show that i ↦ −iσx, j ↦ −iσy, k ↦ −iσz obeys the same rules.

topics.title: SU(3)
topics.goal: The symmetry behind quarks and color.
checks: I can count SU(3) generators and combine triplets.

ex.q: How many generators does SU(n) have? Evaluate for n = 3. What particles correspond to them?
Mesons are a quark plus an antiquark: 3 ⊗ 3̄ = 8 ⊕ 1. Check the dimensions.
Baryons are three quarks: 3 ⊗ 3 ⊗ 3 = 10 ⊕ 8 ⊕ 8 ⊕ 1. Check the dimensions.

topics.title: The Lorentz group
topics.goal: How fields transform in relativity.
checks: I can write boosts with rapidity and count the generators.

ex.q: Write the 1+1D boost matrix with rapidity η using cosh and sinh.
ex.a: [[cosh η, sinh η], [sinh η, cosh η]]

ex.q: Multiply two boosts and show the rapidities add (compare 1.24 and 2.26).
ex.a: The cosh and sinh addition formulas

ex.q: How many generators does the Lorentz group have, and what are they?
ex.a: Six: three rotations and three boosts.

topics.title: Tensors
topics.goal: Tensors as objects that transform predictably.
checks: I can tell vectors from covectors by how they transform.

ex.q: Double the length of your basis vectors. What happens to the components of a vector? Of a gradient (covector)?
ex.a: Vector components halve; gradient components double

ex.q: Write the metric of the plane in polar coordinates.
Contract T^{ij} with δ_{ij}. What do you get?

topics.title: Index notation
topics.goal: Read and manipulate index expressions.
checks: I can read and write expressions with repeated-index summation and the Levi-Civita symbol.

ex.q: Write a · b, A times x, and a × b in index notation.
Use ε_ijk ε_ilm = δ_jl δ_km − δ_jm δ_kl to prove a × (b × c) = b(a · c) − c(a · b).
What is δ_ii in 3D?

topics.title: Covariant derivatives
topics.goal: Derivatives on curved spaces.
checks: I can explain why derivatives need correcting in curved coordinates.

ex.q: Find the Christoffel symbols of the flat plane in polar coordinates.
Carry an arrow around a triangle on a globe, always keeping it "parallel". Does it come back the same?
ex.a: No: it turns by the enclosed curvature.

topics.title: Manifolds
topics.goal: Curved spaces (needed for general relativity).
checks: I can say what makes a space a manifold.

ex.q: Which are manifolds: a circle, a sphere, a torus, a figure-eight?
Why can't a single flat map cover the whole sphere?
ex.a: A sphere is not topologically a plane

ex.q: A triangle on a sphere has three 90° angles. What fraction of the sphere does it cover? Check that the angle excess equals area/R².

topics.title: Differential forms
topics.goal: Coordinate-free integration.
checks: I can use the wedge product and exterior derivative.

ex.q: Show dx ∧ dy = −dy ∧ dx.
Compute d(x dy).
Explain how ∫ dw over a region = ∫ w over its boundary includes Green's, Stokes' and the divergence theorem.

topics.title: Topology
topics.goal: Properties that survive smooth deformation (topological phases).
checks: I can compute simple topological invariants.

ex.q: Compute V − E + F for a cube and for a tetrahedron.
What is the fundamental group of a circle, and what does the integer count?
Why is it impossible to comb a hairy ball flat everywhere?
ex.a: A sphere has Euler characteristic 2, not 0.

topics.title: Fiber bundles and gauge theory
topics.goal: The geometry behind gauge fields and Berry phase.
checks: I can describe a non-trivial bundle and link it to gauge fields.

ex.q: Explain the Möbius strip as a line bundle over a circle. Why is it not just a cylinder?
In one paragraph, explain how the vector potential A acts as a connection and the Berry phase as a holonomy.

topics.title: Clifford and geometric algebra
topics.goal: The algebra behind Dirac's gamma matrices.
checks: I can use the anticommutation relations behind the Dirac matrices.

ex.q: Check that the Pauli matrices satisfy σᵢσⱼ + σⱼσᵢ = 2δᵢⱼ I.
For vectors a and b, the geometric product is ab = a · b + a ∧ b. Compute it for a = e₁ and b = e₁ + e₂.

topics.title: Grassmann numbers
topics.goal: Anticommuting numbers for fermion path integrals.
checks: I can integrate over anticommuting variables.

ex.q: If θ² = 0, write e^θ exactly.
Using ∫ dθ θ = 1 and ∫ dθ 1 = 0, compute ∫ dθ̄ dθ e^(−θ̄ a θ).
Compare with the ordinary Gaussian result √(π/a). What changed, and why does this make fermion path integrals give determinants?
ex.a: The a moved to the numerator; many variables give det(A) instead of 1/√det(A).

topics.title: Functional integration
topics.goal: Integrating over all functions.
checks: I can explain the path integral as a limit of many ordinary integrals.

ex.q: Split a path from 0 to T into N steps. How many ordinary integrals do you need?
Why is each step's integral Gaussian for a free particle?
ex.a: The kinetic term is quadratic in the step

ex.q: What problem does rotating time to imaginary values (Wick rotation) fix?
ex.a: It turns oscillating phases into decaying exponentials.

topics.title: Measure theory
topics.goal: Rigorous probability and integration.
checks: I can explain why some sets have measure zero.

ex.q: Show the rationals in [0, 1] have measure 0 by covering them with tiny intervals.
ex.a: Cover the n-th rational by an interval of length ε/2ⁿ: total ε

ex.q: Show the Cantor set has measure 0 even though it is uncountable.
ex.a: At step n the remaining length is (2/3)ⁿ.

ex.q: Why can't a Riemann integral handle the function that is 1 on rationals and 0 elsewhere?

topics.title: C*-algebras
topics.goal: An operator-algebra view of quantum theory.
checks: I can describe a quantum state as a linear functional on observables.

ex.q: Check ‖A*A‖ = ‖A‖² for A = diag(2, 3i).
Show ω(A) = tr(ρA) is linear and gives ω(I) = 1 for a density matrix ρ.

topics.title: Category theory
topics.goal: The language of the ZX-calculus and some quantum foundations work.
checks: I can name the parts of a category and give an example of a functor.

ex.q: Describe the category of sets: objects, arrows, composition, identities.
Why is "take the fundamental group" a functor?
Look up the ZX-calculus and draw a CNOT gate in it.

parts.name: Classical Mechanics
parts.title: Classical mechanics
parts.intro: Use g = 9.8 m/s² unless told otherwise. Highlight: in 8.34 you find the true path of a thrown ball by minimizing the action yourself.

topics.title: Distance and displacement
topics.goal: Tell distance from displacement.
checks: I can tell distance from displacement.

ex.q: You run one lap of a 400 m track. Find your distance and displacement.
You walk 5 km north then 12 km east. Find your displacement.
Can displacement ever be larger than distance?

topics.title: Speed, velocity and acceleration
topics.goal: Velocity is a vector; acceleration is change in velocity.
checks: I can explain why turning at constant speed is acceleration.

ex.q: A car turns a corner at a steady 50 km/h. Is it accelerating?
A car goes from 0 to 100 km/h in 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s² and in units of g.
You drive to a town at 60 km/h and back at 40 km/h. What is your average speed? (It is not 50.)

topics.title: Kinematic equations
topics.goal: Solve motion problems with the four equations.
checks: I can solve constant-acceleration problems with the four equations.

ex.q: A car at 20 m/s brakes at 5 m/s². How long and how far until it stops?
A stone falls 45 m (use g = 10). How long does it take and how fast does it land?
Derive v² = u² + 2as from the other equations.
A friend drops a ruler and you catch it after it has fallen 20 cm. What is your reaction time?

topics.title: Projectile motion
topics.goal: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
checks: I can treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.

ex.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a 20 m cliff (g = 10). When and where does it land?
At what angle is the range largest on flat ground? What is the range at 20 m/s?
One bullet is dropped and another fired horizontally from the same height. Which lands first?

topics.title: Newton's first law
topics.goal: Objects keep moving unless a force acts.
checks: I can explain everyday effects with inertia.

ex.q: Why do you lurch forward when a bus brakes?
ex.a: Your body keeps moving while the bus slows

ex.q: How does the tablecloth trick work?
An astronaut lets go of a moving wrench in deep space. What does it do?
ex.a: Moves in a straight line at constant speed forever.

topics.title: Newton's second law
topics.goal: Use F = ma, and F = dp/dt.
checks: I can use F = ma and F = dp/dt.

ex.q: What force accelerates a 1200 kg car at 3 m/s²?
A 10 N force acts on 2 kg. Find the acceleration.
A rocket expels 50 kg of gas per second at 3000 m/s. What is its thrust?
A 70 kg person stands on a scale in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s². What does the scale read in newtons?

topics.title: Newton's third law
topics.goal: Forces come in pairs.
checks: I can identify action-reaction pairs and the bodies they act on.

ex.q: If the cart pulls back on the horse as hard as the horse pulls forward, how does anything move?
ex.a: The pair acts on different bodies; the horse moves because the ground pushes it forward

ex.q: Earth pulls an apple with 1 N. How hard does the apple pull Earth, and what is Earth's acceleration (mass 6 × 10²⁴ kg)?
How can a rocket accelerate in empty space with nothing to push on?
ex.a: It pushes the exhaust, which pushes back.

topics.title: Free body diagrams
topics.goal: Draw every force on an object and add them.
checks: I can draw every force on an object and solve for motion.

ex.q: A block slides down a frictionless 30° slope. Find its acceleration.
An Atwood machine hangs 3 kg and 5 kg over a pulley. Find the acceleration and the rope tension.
A 100 N sign hangs from two cables, each 30° above horizontal. Find the tension in each.

topics.title: Friction
topics.goal: Model friction.
checks: I can use static and kinetic friction coefficients.

ex.q: A 10 kg box slides at constant speed with μₖ = 0.3. How hard are you pushing?
A block starts to slide when a ramp reaches 25°. Find μₛ.
Why do anti-lock brakes shorten stopping distance?
ex.a: Rolling tyres use static friction, which is larger.

topics.title: Hooke's law
topics.goal: F = −kx and spring energy ½kx².
checks: I can use F = −kx and ½kx².

ex.q: A spring stretches 5 cm under 10 N. Find k and the stored energy at that stretch.
What is the spring constant of two identical springs in series? In parallel?
A 70 kg bungee jumper hangs at rest on a cord with k = 100 N/m. How far is it stretched?
Why do chemical bonds behave like springs for small stretches? (Use 2.29 Exercise 6.)

topics.title: Circular motion
topics.goal: a = v²/r points inward.
checks: I can use a = v²/r and identify the force that supplies it.

ex.q: A car takes a 50 m radius bend at 20 m/s. Find its acceleration and the friction coefficient it needs.
The ISS circles at radius 6,780 km every 92 minutes. Find its speed and acceleration.
What is the slowest you can swing a bucket overhead in a 1 m circle without spilling?

topics.title: Newton's law of gravitation
topics.goal: F = Gm₁m₂/r².
checks: I can compute gravitational forces and surface gravity.

ex.q: Find the gravitational force between two 70 kg people 1 m apart.
Find g at Earth's surface from G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹, M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and R = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.
Find g at the ISS, 400 km up. So why do astronauts float?
ex.a: About 8.7 m/s²; they are in free fall with the station

ex.q: Compare the electric repulsion and gravitational attraction between two protons. (k = 8.99 × 10⁹, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.)

topics.title: Kepler's laws
topics.goal: Elliptical orbits and equal areas.
checks: I can state all three laws and use T² ∝ a³.

ex.q: Mars orbits at 1.52 AU. How long is its year?
Where in its orbit does a comet move fastest, and why?
Derive T² ∝ r³ for a circular orbit from gravity and circular motion.

topics.title: Escape and orbital velocity
topics.goal: Derive v_esc = √(2GM/r) from energy conservation.
checks: I can derive escape velocity from energy conservation.

ex.q: Find Earth's escape velocity.
Find the speed of a low circular orbit. How does it compare?
At what radius would light itself be unable to escape a mass M? Evaluate it for Earth's mass.

topics.title: Work
topics.goal: Work = force × distance along the motion.
checks: I can compute work, including at an angle.

ex.q: Push with 50 N over 10 m. Find the work if you push along the motion, then at 60° to it.
You carry a bag at constant height and speed. How much work do you do on it? Why are you still tired?
ex.a: Zero; muscles burn energy just holding

ex.q: Find the work to lift 10 kg by 2 m.

topics.title: Conservation of energy
topics.search: kinetic potential energy conservation of energy
topics.goal: Energy is conserved; trade KE for PE.
checks: I can trade kinetic and potential energy to find speeds and heights.

ex.q: A roller coaster drops 45 m from rest. How fast is it at the bottom?
A pendulum bob is released 0.2 m above its lowest point. How fast does it pass the bottom?
A skydiver at terminal speed is losing potential energy but not gaining kinetic energy. Where does the energy go?
ex.a: Into heating and stirring the air

ex.q: A cart rolls from height h into a loop of radius R. Find the smallest h that keeps it on the track at the top.

topics.title: Power
topics.goal: Power is energy per time.
checks: I can compute power and convert energy units.

ex.q: A 70 kg person climbs 3 m of stairs in 4 s. What is their power?
How many joules are in 1 kWh?
A resting human uses about 100 W. How many kilocalories per day is that? (1 kcal = 4184 J.)

topics.title: Momentum and impulse
topics.search: momentum and impulse conservation of momentum
topics.goal: Total momentum is conserved.
checks: I can use impulse = change in momentum.

ex.q: Find the momentum of a 0.15 kg ball at 40 m/s.
A catcher stops it in 0.01 s. What is the average force?
A 4 kg gun fires a 0.01 kg bullet at 400 m/s. How fast does the gun recoil?
Why do airbags reduce injuries?
ex.a: Longer stopping time means smaller force.

topics.title: Collisions
topics.goal: Solve 1D collisions.
checks: I can solve 1D elastic and inelastic collisions.

ex.q: A 1 kg ball at 4 m/s hits an identical ball at rest elastically. Find both final velocities.
The same balls stick together instead. Find the final speed and the kinetic energy lost.
Explain Newton's cradle with Exercise 1.
Hold a tennis ball on top of a basketball and drop them together. The tennis ball bounces far higher. Explain using relative velocity. Estimate how much higher.
ex.a: The tennis ball leaves at about 3 times the speed, reaching about 9 times the height (less in practice).

topics.title: Centre of mass
topics.goal: Motion of a system as one point.
checks: I can find the centre of mass of simple systems.

ex.q: 2 kg sits at x = 0 and 3 kg at x = 5 m. Find the centre of mass.
The Moon (7.35 × 10²² kg) is 384,400 km from Earth (5.97 × 10²⁴ kg). Where is their centre of mass? Is it inside Earth?
ex.a: About 4,670 km from Earth's centre: inside Earth

ex.q: How can a high jumper clear a bar while their centre of mass passes under it?
ex.a: Bending the body puts the centre of mass outside it.

topics.title: Torque and moment of inertia
topics.goal: Rotational version of F = ma.
checks: I can compute torque and use I for rotation.

ex.q: 20 N at the end of a 0.5 m wrench gives what torque?
Compare the moment of inertia of a rod about its middle and about its end.
A solid ball, a solid cylinder and a hoop race down a slope. Predict the order and test it with household objects.
30 kg sits 2 m from a seesaw pivot. Where must 40 kg sit to balance?

topics.title: Angular momentum
topics.goal: L = r × p is conserved; spinning skaters (angular momentum gets quantized later).
checks: I can use conservation of angular momentum.

ex.q: A skater halves her moment of inertia. What happens to her spin rate and her kinetic energy? Where does the extra energy come from?
ex.a: Spin doubles and kinetic energy doubles; from the work her arms do

ex.q: A star of radius 7 × 10⁵ km spinning once every 25 days collapses to 10 km. Estimate its new spin period.
ex.a: About 4 × 10⁻⁴ s (real neutron stars lose spin on the way)

ex.q: Find Earth's orbital angular momentum (m = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, v = 2.98 × 10⁴ m/s, r = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m) in units of ħ = 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴. Why can't we see that angular momentum is quantized?
ex.a: About 2.7 × 10⁴⁰ kg·m²/s ≈ 2.5 × 10⁷⁴ ħ: the steps are far too fine.

topics.title: Gyroscopes and precession
topics.goal: Why a spinning top precesses (later: spin precession in magnetic fields).
checks: I can explain precession with torque = dL/dt.

ex.q: Explain the direction a spinning top precesses using torque as the change in L.
Show the precession rate is mgr/(Iω) for a top.
Earth's axis precesses every 26,000 years. Which torque causes it?
ex.a: The Sun and Moon pulling on Earth's equatorial bulge.

topics.title: The tennis racket theorem
topics.search: Dzhanibekov effect tennis racket theorem Veritasium
topics.goal: Why rotation about the middle axis is unstable.
checks: I can predict which spin axis is unstable.

ex.q: Toss a phone or book spinning about each of its three axes. Which one flips?
Which axis of a book has the middle moment of inertia?
Why doesn't Earth flip like the Dzhanibekov nut?
ex.a: It spins about its largest-moment axis, and friction damps any wobble.

topics.title: Potential energy diagrams
topics.search: potential energy diagrams equilibrium turning points
topics.goal: Read V(x) graphs: wells, barriers, turning points. Quantum problems are posed this way.
checks: I can read wells, barriers and turning points from V(x).

ex.q: For V(x) = x⁴ − 2x², find the minima and the maximum. A particle has E = −0.5. Where can it be? (Quantum mechanics will let it tunnel, 15.14.)
ex.a: Minima at x = ±1 (V = −1), maximum at 0 (V = 0); it stays in one well

ex.q: Find the turning points for V = ½kx² at energy E.
The Lennard-Jones potential is 4ε[(σ/r)¹² − (σ/r)⁶]. Find the equilibrium distance.

topics.title: Simple harmonic motion
topics.goal: ω = √(k/m); period independent of amplitude.
checks: I can find period and frequency for springs and pendulums.

ex.q: A 0.2 kg mass hangs on a 20 N/m spring. Find ω and the period.
How long is a 1 m pendulum's period?
Time 20 swings of a pendulum at home and calculate g.
Find the maximum speed of a mass oscillating with amplitude A.

topics.title: Galilean relativity
topics.goal: Physics is the same in all inertial frames.
checks: I can add velocities between frames the classical way.

ex.q: On a train at 30 m/s you throw a ball forward at 10 m/s. How fast is it relative to the ground?
On a smooth train you drop a ball. Where does it land?
What experiment broke Galilean velocity addition? (See 12.1.)
ex.a: Measurements of the speed of light.

topics.title: Fictitious forces
topics.goal: Forces in rotating frames.
checks: I can explain centrifugal and Coriolis effects.

ex.q: In a turning car you feel pushed outward. Is any real force pushing you outward?
ex.a: No: you keep going straight while the car turns

ex.q: Why do hurricanes spin counterclockwise in the northern hemisphere?
A Foucault pendulum's plane turns once every 24 h/sin(latitude). Find the period in Berlin (52.5° N).

topics.title: Fluids basics
topics.goal: Pressure, Archimedes' principle.
checks: I can compute pressure with depth and use Archimedes' principle.

ex.q: How much extra pressure is there 10 m under water?
Ice has density 917 kg/m³. What fraction of an ice cube is under fresh water?
Why does a steel ship float?
ex.a: Its hull displaces water heavier than the ship.

topics.title: Coupled oscillators
topics.goal: Normal modes are eigenvectors (phonons later).
checks: I can find normal modes as eigenvectors.

ex.q: Two equal masses m are joined to walls and to each other by three springs k. Find the two normal-mode frequencies.
Start with only one mass displaced. Describe how the energy moves (compare beats in 9.7).
ex.a: It sloshes back and forth between the masses

ex.q: What do the normal modes of a chain of N masses become in a solid? (See 17.34.)

topics.title: The two-body problem
topics.goal: Reduce two bodies to one (setup for hydrogen).
checks: I can reduce two bodies to one with the reduced mass.

ex.q: Find the reduced mass of hydrogen as a fraction of the electron mass (proton = 1836 electron masses).
Positronium is an electron orbiting a positron. What is its reduced mass? How should its energy levels compare with hydrogen's?

topics.title: Effective potential
topics.goal: Use the effective potential with the centrifugal term.
checks: I can read bound and unbound orbits from V_eff.

ex.q: For V_eff = −k/r + L²/(2mr²), find the radius of the circular orbit.
Sketch V_eff and mark energies for circular, elliptical and escaping orbits.
How does the centrifugal term keep electrons with angular momentum away from the nucleus? (See 17.1.)

topics.title: Rigid body rotation
topics.goal: Rotation of extended bodies.
checks: I can identify principal axes and stable rotations.

ex.q: What are the principal axes of a rectangular box?
ex.a: The three axes through the centre, parallel to the edges

ex.q: About which axes is free rotation stable? Link this to 8.22.
Why is a thrown rugby ball stable when spiralling about its long axis?
ex.a: Its spin is about an extreme axis.

topics.title: The double pendulum
topics.goal: Deterministic chaos in mechanics.
checks: I can explain chaos in a simple mechanical system.

ex.q: Simulate a double pendulum twice with starting angles 0.001 rad apart. When do the runs visibly separate?
Why is the motion not chaotic for very small swings?
ex.a: Small swings are almost linear, so the motion is two normal modes

ex.q: Is chaotic motion random? Explain.
ex.a: No: it is deterministic but unpredictable in practice.

topics.title: Phase space
topics.goal: A system's state as a point in (q, p) space.
checks: I can draw phase portraits.

ex.q: Draw the phase portrait of a frictionless oscillator.
Add damping. What changes?
Draw it for a free particle.
In quantum mechanics each state takes up about h of phase-space area. How many states fit in an oscillator's ellipse of energy E? (The area is 2πE/ω.)

topics.title: The principle of least action
topics.goal: Nature picks the path that makes the action stationary.
checks: I can explain least action and use it to pick out the real path.

ex.q: A ball (m = 1, g = 10) is thrown up at t = 0 and caught at the same height at t = 2. Try paths x(t) = c t(2 − t). Compute the action S = ∫(½v² − gx) dt from 0 to 2 as a function of c. Which c makes it smallest? Is that the real path?
ex.a: S = 4c²/3 − 40c/3, smallest at c = 5: x = 10t − 5t², the real path

ex.q: Why do physicists say "stationary action" rather than "least"?
ex.a: Sometimes the real path is a saddle, not a minimum.

topics.title: Lagrangian mechanics
topics.goal: L = T − V and generalized coordinates.
checks: I can write L = T − V and derive equations of motion.

ex.q: Write L for a mass on a spring and derive its equation of motion.
Write L for a pendulum in terms of θ and derive θ″ = −(g/L) sin θ.
Write L for a free particle in polar coordinates.

topics.title: Deriving the Euler-Lagrange equations
topics.goal: Derive equations of motion from L.
checks: I can derive the equations from varying the path.

ex.q: Vary x(t) by a small δx(t) that vanishes at the ends and derive the Euler-Lagrange equation.
Apply it to L = ½mẋ² − V(x).
If L does not depend on some coordinate q, what is conserved?

topics.title: Constraints and generalized coordinates
topics.goal: Handle pendulums and beads on wires.
checks: I can choose good coordinates for constrained systems.

ex.q: Write L for an Atwood machine using one coordinate.
ex.a: L = ½(m₁ + m₂)ẋ² + (m₁ − m₂)gx (for x measured down on m₁)

ex.q: Write L for a bead on a hoop of radius R spinning at ω about its vertical diameter.
ex.a: L = ½mR²(θ̇² + ω² sin²θ) + mgR cos θ.

ex.q: Write L for a pendulum hanging from a cart that slides freely.

topics.title: Noether's theorem
topics.goal: Each symmetry gives a conserved quantity.
checks: I can match symmetries to conserved quantities.

ex.q: Match: time shifts, position shifts, rotations. Conserved: angular momentum, energy, momentum.
ex.a: Time: energy; position: momentum; rotation: angular momentum

ex.q: For a central force, why is angular momentum conserved?
ex.a: L does not depend on the angle

ex.q: In an expanding universe, light loses energy as it redshifts. Which symmetry is missing?

topics.title: Hamiltonian mechanics
topics.goal: H = T + V, canonical momentum, Hamilton's equations. H becomes the quantum Hamiltonian.
checks: I can write H and Hamilton's equations.

ex.q: Write H for a mass on a spring and show Hamilton's equations give F = ma.
ex.a: H = p²/2m + ½kx²; ẋ = p/m, ṗ = −kx

ex.q: Write H for a pendulum.
Sketch the flow Hamilton's equations draw in phase space for the pendulum.

topics.title: The Legendre transformation
topics.goal: Move from L to H.
checks: I can move from L to H.

ex.q: From L = ½mẋ² − V, find p and H = pẋ − L.
Which thermodynamic quantity is the Legendre transform of internal energy with respect to entropy? (See 10.20.)
ex.a: Helmholtz free energy F = U − TS.

topics.title: Poisson brackets
topics.goal: {x, p} = 1 becomes [x, p] = iħ in quantum mechanics.
checks: I can compute Poisson brackets and know how they turn into commutators.

ex.q: Compute {x, p}.
Compute {x, H} and {p, H} for H = p²/2m + V(x). What do they give?
Compute {L_x, L_y}.
Dirac's rule is {A, B} → [A, B]/(iħ). What does {x, p} = 1 become?

topics.title: Liouville's theorem
topics.goal: Phase-space volume is conserved.
checks: I can explain why phase-space volume is conserved.

ex.q: A cloud of oscillators fills a small square in phase space. Describe its shape after a quarter period and its area.
Why can't mirrors and lenses alone cool a particle beam? How does laser cooling get around this?
ex.a: Lenses conserve phase-space volume; laser cooling dumps entropy into scattered light.

topics.title: Canonical transformations
topics.goal: Change variables while keeping Hamilton's equations.
checks: I can check that new variables keep {Q, P} = 1.

ex.q: Check that Q = p, P = −x is canonical.
For an oscillator, define the angle variable as the phase of the motion. What is its conjugate momentum? (See 8.45.)

topics.title: The Hamilton-Jacobi equation
topics.goal: The classical equation closest to the Schrödinger equation.
checks: I can solve it for a free particle and connect it to waves.

ex.q: Show S = px − p²t/(2m) solves ∂S/∂t + (1/2m)(∂S/∂x)² = 0.
Compare e^(iS/ħ) with a quantum plane wave. What do you notice?
ex.a: It is a plane wave with momentum p and energy p²/2m.

topics.title: Action-angle variables and adiabatic invariants
topics.goal: The basis of the old quantum theory (Bohr-Sommerfeld).
checks: I can compute the action J = ∮ p dx and explain why it was quantized first.

ex.q: Show J = 2πE/ω for an oscillator.
A pendulum's string is shortened very slowly. What stays constant?
Bohr and Sommerfeld set J = nh. What energies does this give the oscillator? What does the full quantum answer add?
ex.a: E = nħω; the full answer adds ½ħω.

topics.title: The Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector
topics.goal: The hidden symmetry that later explains hydrogen's degeneracy.
checks: I can explain why Kepler orbits do not precess.

ex.q: Show the vector p × L − mk r̂ points toward the closest approach in an elliptical orbit.
Mercury's orbit precesses by about 43″ per century more than Newton predicts. What does that tell you about the force law?
ex.a: The force is not exactly 1/r²; general relativity explains the difference.

topics.title: A full classical mechanics course
topics.goal: A full lecture course on all of the above.
checks: I can solve mixed problems with Lagrangians, Hamiltonians and brackets.

ex.q: Derive the orbit equation for a central force from the Lagrangian in polar coordinates.
Find the equilibrium positions of a bead on a hoop spinning at ω (8.37 Exercise 2). When does the bottom stop being stable?
ex.a: θ = 0, and cos θ = g/(Rω²) once ω² > g/R, when the bottom becomes unstable

ex.q: Compute {L_z, x} with L_z = xp_y − yp_x.

parts.name: Waves and Optics
parts.title: Waves, oscillations and optics
parts.intro: Use hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm and the speed of sound 343 m/s. Highlight: in 9.26 you find that a matter wave's group velocity is exactly the particle's classical velocity.

topics.title: What a wave is
topics.search: what is a wave transverse longitudinal
topics.goal: Waves carry energy, not matter.
checks: I can tell transverse from longitudinal waves and say what a wave carries.

ex.q: In a stadium wave, does anyone travel around the stadium?
Classify as transverse, longitudinal or both: sound in air, light, a guitar string, ocean surface waves, earthquake P and S waves.
ex.a: Longitudinal; transverse; transverse; both; P longitudinal and S transverse

ex.q: What does a wave transport, and what does it leave behind?
ex.a: Energy and momentum; the medium stays put.

topics.title: Wavelength, frequency and speed
topics.goal: Use v = fλ.
checks: I can use v = fλ in any unit.

ex.q: Find the wavelength of a 440 Hz note in air.
Find the wavelength of 100 MHz FM radio.
Find the frequency of 530 nm green light.

Take the turntable out of a microwave oven (2.45 GHz), heat a plate of chocolate briefly, and measure the gap between melted spots. They are half a wavelength apart. Compute the speed of light from your measurement.
ex.a: Spots about 6.1 cm apart give c = 2 × 0.061 m × 2.45 × 10⁹ Hz ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

topics.title: Superposition
topics.goal: Waves add point by point. This is the core idea behind quantum superposition.
checks: I can add waves point by point and say when superposition holds.

ex.q: Two pulses on a rope run into each other. What happens after they pass?
Add 2 sin x and −sin x.
Give an example where superposition fails.
ex.a: Very large water waves, or intense light in some crystals

ex.q: In quantum mechanics, ψ₁ + ψ₂ is also a valid state. Which property of the Schrödinger equation makes that true?

topics.title: Interference
topics.goal: Path difference decides bright or dark.
checks: I can predict bright and dark spots from path differences.

ex.q: Two speakers emit a 343 Hz tone in step. You stand 3 m from one and 3.5 m from the other. Loud or quiet?
ex.a: λ = 1 m and the path difference is half of it: quiet

ex.q: How do noise-cancelling headphones work?
ex.a: They add sound in opposite phase

ex.q: Write the conditions for constructive and destructive interference in terms of the path difference.

topics.title: Standing waves
topics.search: standing waves harmonics on a string
topics.goal: Fixed ends allow only certain wavelengths. This is how quantization arises.
checks: I can find the allowed wavelengths on strings and in pipes.

ex.q: A string is 0.6 m long with fixed ends. List the three longest allowed wavelengths.
Where are the nodes of the third harmonic?
Why does a pipe closed at one end only play odd harmonics?
ex.a: The closed end needs a node and the open end an antinode

ex.q: Blow across a bottle while adding water. Why does the pitch rise?

topics.title: Resonance
topics.goal: Driving at a natural frequency builds large amplitude.
checks: I can explain resonance and spot it in everyday life.

ex.q: When should you push a child on a swing, and why?
ex.a: Once per swing at the same point, in step with its natural rhythm

ex.q: How can a singer break a wine glass?
Microwave ovens are often said to heat water "at its resonant frequency". Is that true?
ex.a: No: it heats by rotating water molecules over a broad range of frequencies

ex.q: An MRI scanner works by resonance. What is resonating? (See 13.36.)
ex.a: Nuclear spins in the magnetic field.

topics.title: Beats
topics.goal: Two close frequencies produce beats.
checks: I can predict beat frequencies and derive them.

ex.q: Tones of 440 Hz and 444 Hz play together. How many beats per second?
Derive the beat pattern from 1.24 Exercise 4.
Explain how musicians tune by listening for beats.
ex.a: Beats slow down and vanish when the two notes match.

topics.title: The Doppler effect
topics.goal: Frequency shifts with motion.
checks: I can compute Doppler shifts for moving sources.

ex.q: A 700 Hz siren approaches at 30 m/s, then moves away. What frequencies do you hear?
Why is light from distant galaxies redshifted? (See 12.28.)
Atoms can be slowed with lasers tuned slightly below their resonance. Why does the Doppler effect make this work? (See 17.51.)
ex.a: Atoms moving toward the laser see it shifted up into resonance and get pushed back.

topics.title: Sound
topics.goal: Sound as pressure waves.
checks: I can work with sound speeds, wavelengths and frequency ranges.

ex.q: Thunder arrives 3 s after the lightning. How far away is the storm?
Humans hear from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz. What range of wavelengths is that?
Why can't sound travel through space?

topics.title: Chladni plates
topics.goal: 2D standing waves (a visual cousin of atomic orbitals).
checks: I can connect 2D standing-wave patterns to their frequencies.

ex.q: Make Chladni figures with a speaker, a metal plate (or a stretched balloon) and salt. Photograph three frequencies.
How does the number of nodal lines change with frequency?
Atomic orbitals also have nodes. How many radial nodes does a 2s orbital have? (See 5.25.)

topics.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
topics.goal: Radio to gamma rays: wavelength, frequency, energy.
checks: I can order the spectrum and convert wavelength to photon energy.

ex.q: Order from longest to shortest wavelength: gamma, visible, radio, X-ray, microwave, ultraviolet, infrared.
ex.a: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma

ex.q: Find the photon energy of 500 nm light in eV.
Find the wavelength of a 1 keV X-ray photon.
Why does UV light burn skin while far more intense radio waves do not? (See 24.9b.)
ex.a: Each UV photon carries enough energy to break bonds; radio photons do not.

topics.title: Reflection and refraction
topics.goal: Light bends at boundaries.
checks: I can use Snell's law and n = c/v.

ex.q: Light enters water (n = 1.33) at 45°. Find the refracted angle.
How fast does light travel in glass with n = 1.5?
Why does a straw look bent in a glass of water?
ex.a: Light from the underwater part bends at the surface.

ex.q: Link Snell's law to 2.12 Exercise 4.

topics.title: Why light slows down in glass
topics.search: why light slows down in glass 3Blue1Brown
topics.goal: Refractive index from electrons shaking.
checks: I can explain the refractive index as interference between incoming and re-radiated light.

ex.q: Explain in your own words, without photons, why light appears slower in glass.
Why does n depend on colour, and what does that do in a prism?
ex.a: The electrons' response depends on frequency, so colours separate.

topics.title: Total internal reflection
topics.goal: Light trapped by reflection.
checks: I can find critical angles.

ex.q: Find the critical angle from glass (n = 1.5) to air.
Find it from water to air.
Diamond has n = 2.42. Find its critical angle. Why does this make diamonds sparkle?
ex.a: About 24.4°: light bounces around inside many times

ex.q: Why is internet traffic carried by light in glass fibres?
ex.a: Light is trapped by total internal reflection and carries huge bandwidth.

topics.title: Lenses and mirrors
topics.goal: Find images with ray diagrams.
checks: I can locate images with 1/f = 1/u + 1/v and ray diagrams.

ex.q: A lens with f = 10 cm images an object 30 cm away. Where is the image, and how big is it?
ex.a: 15 cm behind the lens, half size, inverted

ex.q: Move the object to 5 cm. What kind of image do you get now?
ex.a: Virtual, upright and magnified, 10 cm on the same side

ex.q: Why does a make-up mirror magnify?
ex.a: The face sits inside the focal length of a concave mirror.

topics.title: Fermat's principle
topics.goal: Light takes the quickest path (an early least-action principle).
checks: I can explain reflection and refraction as least-time paths.

ex.q: A lifeguard runs fast on sand and swims slowly. Why is the fastest path to a swimmer bent, and how does it relate to Snell's law?
ex.a: Time is minimized when sin θ₁/v₁ = sin θ₂/v₂

ex.q: Explain a road mirage with Fermat's principle.
ex.a: Light curves through hot air near the road, where it is faster.

ex.q: How does Fermat's principle foreshadow 8.34 and 15.32?

topics.title: Huygens' principle
topics.goal: Every point on a wavefront acts as a new source.
checks: I can build wavefronts from wavelets.

ex.q: Derive the law of reflection with Huygens wavelets.
Derive Snell's law the same way.
Why do waves bend around obstacles?
ex.a: Wavelets from the edge spread into the shadow.

topics.title: Single-slit diffraction
topics.goal: Narrower slit, wider spread.
checks: I can find the width of a diffraction pattern.

ex.q: 500 nm light passes a 0.1 mm slit. Find the angle of the first dark fringe and its distance from the centre on a screen 2 m away.
Make the slit narrower. What happens to the pattern? Connect this to 5.14.
ex.a: It spreads more: narrow in space means wide in angle

ex.q: Why can you hear someone around a corner but not see them?
ex.a: Sound wavelengths are metres, light wavelengths under a micrometre.

topics.title: Young's double slit
topics.goal: Derive the fringe spacing classically.
checks: I can derive and use the fringe spacing λL/d.

ex.q: 633 nm light, slits 0.25 mm apart, screen 1 m away. Find the fringe spacing.
Cut two parallel slits in kitchen foil with a razor and shine a laser pointer through. Measure your fringes and estimate the slit spacing.
Cover one slit. What pattern remains?

topics.title: Diffraction gratings
topics.goal: Split light into wavelengths.
checks: I can use d sin θ = mλ.

ex.q: A CD's tracks are 1.6 μm apart. At what angle does 650 nm red light appear in first order?
Why do CDs show rainbows?
ex.a: Each colour diffracts at its own angle

ex.q: A grating has 600 lines per mm. Find the first-order angle for 500 nm light and the highest order you can see.

topics.title: Thin-film interference
topics.goal: Colors from interference.
checks: I can explain colours in soap films and coatings.

ex.q: A soap film has n = 1.33. What is the thinnest film that strongly reflects 550 nm light? (Reflection off the front surface flips the phase.)
Why does a soap bubble turn black just before it pops?
ex.a: The film is far thinner than a wavelength and the two reflections cancel

ex.q: Why are camera lenses coated with a quarter-wavelength layer?
ex.a: Reflections from its two surfaces cancel.

topics.title: Polarization
topics.goal: Light as a transverse wave with direction.
checks: I can explain polarizers and why sound has no polarization.

ex.q: Why do polarized sunglasses cut glare from water?
What passes through two crossed polarizers?
Can sound be polarized?

topics.title: The three-polarizer paradox
topics.goal: Adding a middle filter lets more light through; your first taste of quantum measurement.
checks: I can explain how adding a polarizer lets more light through.

ex.q: Unpolarized light passes crossed polarizers with a third at 45° in between. What fraction gets through?
Use N polarizers in equal steps from 0° to 90°. Find the fraction transmitted for N = 10. What happens as N grows? (This is the quantum Zeno effect in disguise, 19.19.)
Describe the same experiment one photon at a time. What is random, and what is not?
ex.a: Whether each photon passes is random; the probability at each step is cos² of the step angle.

topics.title: Malus's law
topics.goal: Intensity through a polarizer goes as cos²θ (same rule as quantum probabilities).
checks: I can use I = I₀ cos²θ.

ex.q: Polarized light meets a polarizer at 60°. What fraction passes?
What fraction passes at 30°?
For single photons, cos²θ becomes a probability. Which quantum rule is this? (See 15.4.)

topics.title: The Michelson interferometer
topics.goal: Measure tiny distances with interference (LIGO, relativity).
checks: I can convert fringe counts to distances.

ex.q: How far must one mirror move to shift the pattern by one fringe?
You count 1000 fringes with 633 nm light. How far did the mirror move?
LIGO measures arm changes of about 10⁻¹⁸ m. What fraction of a proton's width (about 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m) is that?

topics.title: Wave packets and group velocity
topics.search: wave packets group velocity phase velocity
topics.goal: A localized wave as many frequencies combined.
checks: I can tell group velocity from phase velocity and compute both.

ex.q: Plot cos(10x) + cos(11x). What shape appears?
ex.a: A wave with a slowly varying envelope (beats)

ex.q: Deep water waves have ω = √(gk). Compare their group and phase velocities.
ex.a: The group velocity is half the phase velocity

ex.q: A quantum free particle has ω = ħk²/(2m). Find its group velocity and phase velocity. Which one equals the classical velocity p/m?
ex.a: v_g = ħk/m = p/m and v_p = half of that: the group velocity.

topics.title: Dispersion
topics.goal: Speed depending on frequency makes packets spread.
checks: I can explain how dispersion spreads pulses.

ex.q: Which colour bends most in a glass prism?
Why do short pulses in an optical fibre spread out?
ex.a: Different frequencies travel at different speeds

ex.q: Why does a free quantum wave packet spread (15.18)?
ex.a: Its frequencies travel at different speeds.

topics.title: Coherence
topics.goal: When waves can interfere.
checks: I can estimate coherence lengths.

ex.q: Why don't two separate light bulbs make interference fringes?
ex.a: Their phases are random and uncorrelated

ex.q: Coherence length is about c/Δf. Estimate it for a laser with Δf = 1 MHz and for sunlight with Δf ≈ 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Why do thin soap films show colours but a thick window does not?
ex.a: Its thickness is far above sunlight's coherence length.

topics.title: Evanescent waves
topics.search: evanescent waves frustrated total internal reflection
topics.goal: A classical version of quantum tunneling.
checks: I can explain frustrated total internal reflection as classical tunneling.

ex.q: Two glass prisms are brought within a wavelength of each other. What happens to light that would be totally reflected?
ex.a: Some light tunnels across the gap

ex.q: About how far does the evanescent wave reach?
Which quantum effect does this mimic, and how? (See 15.14.)

topics.title: Birefringence and wave plates
topics.goal: How optics labs prepare polarization states (qubits).
checks: I can describe what quarter- and half-wave plates do.

ex.q: Why does a calcite crystal show a double image?
ex.a: It has two refractive indices for two polarizations

ex.q: What does a quarter-wave plate at 45° do to linearly polarized light?
A half-wave plate at angle θ rotates the polarization by how much?
If polarization is a qubit, what do these plates do on the Bloch sphere (16.18)?

topics.title: Holography
topics.goal: Storing phase information with interference.
checks: I can explain how a hologram records phase as well as brightness.

ex.q: Why does a hologram look 3D while a photo does not?
ex.a: It records the full wavefront including phase

ex.q: Cut a hologram in half. What does each half show?
ex.a: The whole scene, from a narrower range of viewpoints.

topics.title: Solitons
topics.goal: Waves that keep their shape.
checks: I can explain how solitons keep their shape.

ex.q: Look up John Scott Russell's 1834 canal wave. What did he see?
ex.a: A single smooth hump travelling kilometres without changing shape

ex.q: Which two effects balance in a soliton?

topics.title: Fourier optics
topics.goal: Lenses perform Fourier transforms.
checks: I can explain a diffraction pattern as a Fourier transform.

ex.q: A lens forms the Fourier transform of a grating at its focal plane. What do you see there?
Block the outer part of that pattern and reform the image. What changes?
ex.a: Fine detail and sharp edges are lost

ex.q: Photo 51 is an X-ray diffraction pattern of DNA. What was Fourier-transformed to make it, and what did the X shape reveal?
ex.a: The electron density of DNA; it revealed a helix.

parts.name: Thermodynamics
parts.title: Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics
parts.intro: Use k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K and kT ≈ 0.0259 eV at 300 K. Highlight: in 10.4 you find out why helium refuses to freeze at normal pressure, even at absolute zero.

topics.title: Temperature
topics.goal: Temperature tracks the average kinetic energy of particles.
checks: I can link temperature to molecular kinetic energy and convert scales.

ex.q: Convert 300 K to °C and °F.
Find the average kinetic energy (3/2)kT of an air molecule at 300 K, in J and in eV.
Why does kT ≈ 1/40 eV at room temperature explain why chemistry happens at room temperature but nuclear reactions do not?
ex.a: Bonds take a few eV, so thermal tails can break some; nuclear reactions need MeV.

topics.title: Heat and heat capacity
topics.search: heat vs temperature specific heat capacity
topics.goal: Use Q = mcΔT.
checks: I can use Q = mcΔT.

ex.q: How much heat warms 1 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C? (c = 4186 J/(kg·K).)
How long does a 2 kW kettle take?
Why do coastal towns have milder winters?
ex.a: Water's large heat capacity buffers temperature.

topics.title: Phase changes and latent heat
topics.search: states of matter and phase changes latent heat
topics.goal: Energy goes into changing phase at constant temperature.
checks: I can include latent heat in energy calculations.

ex.q: Melting 1 kg of ice takes 334 kJ. Compare with heating 1 kg of water from 0 °C.
ex.a: The same as heating water by about 80 °C

ex.q: Boiling 1 kg of water takes 2.26 MJ. Compare with 10.2 Exercise 1.
Why are steam burns worse than burns from boiling water?
ex.a: Condensing steam releases 2.26 MJ/kg onto the skin.

topics.title: Heat transfer
topics.goal: The three ways heat moves, with an everyday example of each.
checks: I can tell conduction, convection and radiation apart.

ex.q: Classify: a hot pan handle, a pot of boiling soup, sunlight warming your face.
How does a vacuum flask block all three?
ex.a: Vacuum stops conduction and convection; silvering stops radiation

ex.q: Metal and wood at the same temperature feel different. Why?
ex.a: Metal conducts heat away from your skin faster.

topics.title: Phase diagrams
topics.search: phase diagrams triple point critical point
topics.goal: Read a phase diagram (helium's is very unusual).
checks: I can read a phase diagram, including helium's strange one.

ex.q: Water's triple point is 0.01 °C at 611 Pa. What happens there?
Why is pressure melting alone not enough to explain ice skating?
ex.a: The pressure is too small; a thin liquid surface layer matters more

ex.q: Helium stays liquid down to absolute zero unless squeezed to about 25 atm. Explain why using zero-point energy (15.17) and helium's weak attractions.
ex.a: Its zero-point motion is larger than its weak binding, so it cannot settle into a lattice.

topics.title: The ideal gas law
topics.goal: Use the gas law in moles and in molecules (k_B).
checks: I can use PV = nRT and PV = NkT.

ex.q: Find the volume of 1 mol of gas at 0 °C and 1 atm.
A tyre at 10 °C warms to 40 °C at fixed volume. By what factor does its absolute pressure rise?
How many molecules are in 1 m³ of air at 20 °C and 1 atm?

topics.title: Kinetic theory
topics.goal: Derive pressure from molecules hitting walls.
checks: I can derive gas pressure from molecules hitting walls.

ex.q: Derive P = ⅓ρv²_rms.
Find v_rms of nitrogen (28 u, 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) at 300 K.
Why do helium balloons go flat faster than air balloons?
ex.a: Lighter atoms move faster and leak through the rubber.

topics.title: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
topics.goal: Molecules have a spread of speeds.
checks: I can sketch the speed distribution and how it changes with temperature.

ex.q: Sketch the distribution at 300 K and 600 K.
ex.a: The hotter curve is lower, wider and shifted right

ex.q: Order the most probable, average and rms speeds.
Why has Earth lost almost all its hydrogen and helium?
ex.a: The fast tail of light molecules exceeds escape velocity.

topics.title: The first law
topics.search: zeroth and first law of thermodynamics
topics.goal: Energy conservation with heat and work.
checks: I can use ΔU = Q − W.

ex.q: A gas absorbs 500 J and does 200 J of work. Find ΔU.
Why does a bike pump get hot?
ex.a: Work done on the gas heats it

ex.q: An ideal gas expands freely into a vacuum. What happens to its temperature?

topics.title: The second law
topics.goal: Heat flows hot to cold; entropy of an isolated system rises.
checks: I can state the second law in several ways.

ex.q: Why doesn't heat flow from cold to hot by itself?
Why can no engine turn heat from one reservoir entirely into work?
Does a fridge break the second law?
ex.a: No: it uses work and dumps more heat outside.

topics.title: Entropy
topics.goal: Entropy as the number of ways to arrange things.
checks: I can explain entropy as counting arrangements and compute simple entropy changes.

ex.q: 100 coins: compare the number of arrangements with all heads and with 50 heads (use 1.32 Exercise 5).
Find the entropy change when 1 kg of ice melts at 273 K.
Earth absorbs sunlight from a 5800 K source and radiates at about 288 K. Roughly how many infrared photons leave for each visible photon arriving? Why does this matter for life?
ex.a: About 20; the outgoing radiation carries far more entropy, which drives order on Earth.

topics.title: Heat engines and the Carnot limit
topics.goal: Maximum efficiency 1 − T_cold/T_hot.
checks: I can compute Carnot efficiencies.

ex.q: Find the maximum efficiency of an engine between 600 K and 300 K.
Why do real car engines reach only 25 to 30%?
ex.a: Friction, heat loss and fast, irreversible cycles

ex.q: A heat pump warms a 20 °C house from 0 °C outside. What is its ideal coefficient of performance?

topics.title: The third law
topics.search: third law of thermodynamics absolute zero
topics.goal: Why absolute zero cannot be reached.
checks: I can explain why absolute zero is unreachable.

ex.q: What happens to entropy as T → 0?
Why would reaching exactly 0 K take infinitely many cooling steps?
ex.a: Each step removes a smaller fraction of the remaining heat

ex.q: Look up the coldest temperature reached in a lab. How was it done?
ex.a: Below a nanokelvin, using laser and evaporative cooling of atoms.

topics.title: Refrigerators and heat pumps
topics.goal: Moving heat uphill with work.
checks: I can explain the cooling cycle.

ex.q: Explain the four steps of a fridge's compressor cycle.
Why does leaving a fridge door open warm the kitchen?
ex.a: The motor's work adds heat to the kitchen

ex.q: A fridge removes 300 J/s from inside using 100 W. How much heat goes out the back?

topics.title: The Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien laws
topics.search: Stefan-Boltzmann law and Wien's displacement law
topics.goal: Radiated power grows as T⁴; peak wavelength shrinks as 1/T.
checks: I can use P ∝ T⁴ and λ_peak = (2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K)/T.

ex.q: Find the peak wavelength of sunlight (5800 K).
Find it for the human body (310 K). Which camera sees that?
How much more power does a body radiate if its temperature doubles?
Find the peak wavelength of the cosmic background at 2.725 K.

topics.title: Microstates and S = k ln W
topics.search: microstates macrostates Boltzmann entropy S = k log W
topics.goal: Count microstates to get entropy.
checks: I can count microstates and compute entropy.

ex.q: Four coins show two heads. How many microstates? What is S?
Two blocks share energy. Explain with microstate counting why energy flows until they reach the same temperature.
ex.a: Total arrangements are largest when temperatures are equal

ex.q: Find S for 100 coins at exactly 50 heads, in units of k.

topics.title: The Boltzmann factor
topics.goal: Probability of a state at temperature T.
checks: I can use e^(−E/kT) to compare populations.

ex.q: Two levels are 0.1 eV apart. At 300 K, what fraction of atoms sit in the upper one compared with the lower?
Air density falls by e every kT/(mg) of height. Estimate this scale height for nitrogen at 290 K, and the height over which density halves.
ex.a: About 8.5 km; it halves every about 6 km

ex.q: Why does heating populate excited states?
ex.a: kT becomes comparable to the gaps.

topics.title: The partition function
topics.goal: Get every thermodynamic quantity from Z.
checks: I can compute Z and average energy for simple systems.

ex.q: A two-level system has energies 0 and ε. Find Z and the average energy.
What does the average energy tend to as T → 0 and T → ∞?
A quantum oscillator has levels (n + ½)ħω. Sum its partition function using 1.30 Exercise 6.

topics.title: Equipartition
topics.goal: Each quadratic degree of freedom gets ½kT, and where this fails (a quantum clue).
checks: I can predict classical heat capacities and know where they fail.

ex.q: Predict the molar heat capacity at constant volume for a monatomic gas.
Predict it for a diatomic gas. Measured air gives (5/2)R. Which motion is missing?
Predict the heat capacity of a solid (Dulong-Petit).

topics.title: Freezing out degrees of freedom
topics.search: heat capacity of gases freezing out degrees of freedom
