topics.goal: Why rotations and vibrations "switch off" at low T (quantum energy gaps).
checks: I can explain why some motions do not store heat at low temperatures.

ex.q: Hydrogen's rotations switch on near 85 K and vibrations near 6000 K. What heat capacity do you expect at 300 K?
Why was this a deep puzzle for classical physics around 1900?
ex.a: Classical physics says every motion should share energy equally

ex.q: Explain it with quantum energy gaps and kT.
ex.a: If kT is far below the gap, the motion stays in its ground state.

topics.title: Einstein and Debye models
topics.search: Einstein solid and Debye model heat capacity
topics.goal: Quantum explanation of solids' heat capacity.
checks: I can explain the low-temperature heat capacity of solids.

ex.q: Use 10.16 Exercise 3 to find the average energy of a quantum oscillator. Show it tends to kT at high temperature.
How does the Einstein model's heat capacity behave at low T? How does Debye's?
ex.a: Einstein drops exponentially; Debye as T³

ex.q: Diamond has a very low heat capacity at room temperature. Why?
ex.a: Its stiff, light lattice has very high vibration frequencies.

topics.title: Free energy
topics.goal: Which quantity is minimized at equilibrium.
checks: I can use F = U − TS and G = H − TS to predict what happens.

ex.q: Ice melts above 0 °C even though melting absorbs heat. Explain with ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
A rubber band warms up when stretched quickly. Why? (Hint: its chains become more ordered.)
ex.a: Lower entropy of aligned chains releases heat.

topics.title: Chemical potential
topics.goal: The energy cost of adding a particle.
checks: I can explain chemical potential as the push particles feel.

ex.q: Which way do particles flow between regions of different μ?
ex.a: From high μ to low μ

ex.q: Why is the chemical potential of photons zero?
What happens to μ in a Bose gas as it condenses? (See 17.49.)

topics.title: Ensembles
topics.goal: Pick the right ensemble.
checks: I can choose the right ensemble.

ex.q: Match each to an ensemble: a sealed insulated box; a sealed box in a bath; an open box in a bath.
Why do all ensembles give the same answers for very large systems?

topics.title: The Gibbs paradox
topics.goal: Classical counting fails unless identical particles are truly identical (a quantum hint).
checks: I can explain why identical particles must be counted differently.

ex.q: Remove a wall between two halves of the same gas. Should the entropy change? What does naive counting say?
ex.a: No; naive counting gives an increase of 2Nk ln 2

ex.q: Show that dividing the number of states by N! fixes it.
Why does quantum mechanics make that N! natural? (See 17.10.)

topics.title: Brownian motion
topics.search: Brownian motion Einstein proof atoms exist
topics.goal: How random jiggling proved atoms are real.
checks: I can explain how jiggling pollen proved atoms exist.

ex.q: Einstein showed ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt. If a grain wanders 10 μm in 10 s, how far in 40 s?
How did Perrin use this to measure Avogadro's number?
Watch diluted milk under a cheap microscope. Describe what the fat droplets do.

topics.title: Maxwell's demon
topics.goal: Information has a thermodynamic cost (Landauer's principle).
checks: I can explain why the demon does not break the second law.

ex.q: Landauer: erasing one bit releases at least kT ln 2 of heat. Compute it at 300 K.
Describe Szilard's one-molecule engine.
Where does the demon pay its entropy bill?

topics.title: The arrow of time
topics.search: arrow of time entropy Sean Carroll
topics.goal: Why the past differs from the future.
checks: I can explain why the past differs from the future though the laws do not care.

ex.q: Film a breaking glass and play it backwards. Which laws of motion are broken?
Why must the early universe have had very low entropy?
Is wavefunction collapse another arrow of time? Write your guess; revisit in Part 19.

topics.title: Phase transitions
topics.goal: Order parameters and critical exponents.
checks: I can tell first-order from continuous transitions and name an order parameter.

ex.q: Classify boiling water and a magnet losing its magnetism at the Curie point.
What is critical opalescence?
ex.a: Milky scattering near the critical point

ex.q: What is the order parameter of a magnet? Of a superfluid?

topics.title: The Ising model
topics.goal: The simplest model of magnetism and phase transitions.
checks: I can simulate the Ising model and find its transition.

ex.q: Code a 2D Ising model with the Metropolis algorithm and plot the magnetization against temperature.
Compare your critical temperature with Onsager's exact kT_c/J = 2/ln(1 + √2).
Why does the 1D Ising model have no transition?
ex.a: Any domain wall costs finite energy but gains entropy.

topics.title: Mean field theory
topics.goal: Approximate many interacting particles.
checks: I can solve a mean-field self-consistency equation.

ex.q: Mean-field Ising gives m = tanh(βJzm). At what βJz does a non-zero solution first appear?
Why does mean field get the critical behaviour wrong in 2D?

topics.title: The renormalization group
topics.goal: Physics at different scales (also central to quantum field theory).
checks: I can explain universality and coarse-graining.

ex.q: Explain the block-spin idea in a paragraph.
Water at its critical point and a magnet at its Curie point share the same critical exponents. Why is that remarkable?
ex.a: Completely different microscopic physics gives identical numbers

ex.q: Which quantum field theory idea is the same thing (20.24)?

topics.title: Negative temperature
topics.goal: Systems hotter than infinite temperature.
checks: I can explain why negative temperatures are hotter than infinite temperature.

ex.q: In a two-level system, more particles are up than down. Use the Boltzmann factor to show T must be negative.
Which device relies on such a population inversion?

topics.title: The fluctuation-dissipation theorem
topics.goal: Noise and friction are linked.
checks: I can link noise to friction.

ex.q: Johnson noise gives V² = 4kTRΔf. Find the rms noise of a 1 kΩ resistor at 300 K over 10 kHz.
Why does every resistor make noise but a perfect superconductor does not?
ex.a: It has no resistance to dissipate.

topics.title: The Jarzynski equality
topics.goal: Exact results far from equilibrium.
checks: I can state the equality and explain what it means for fluctuations.

ex.q: Write the Jarzynski equality.
Why must some runs of an experiment need less work than ΔF?
ex.a: The average of e^(−βW) needs some runs with W < ΔF.

ex.q: Look up how stretching single RNA molecules tested it.

parts.name: Electromagnetism
parts.title: Electricity and magnetism
parts.intro: Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m and μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. Highlight: in 11.18 you compute the speed of light from two electrical constants.

topics.title: Electric charge
topics.goal: Two kinds of charge; charge is conserved.
checks: I can explain charging by rubbing and why charge is conserved and quantized.

ex.q: A rubbed balloon sticks to a neutral wall. Why?
ex.a: The balloon polarizes the wall's molecules, and the nearer opposite charges win

ex.q: What is the total charge of one mole of electrons?
Quarks carry ±1/3 and ±2/3 of e. Why is charge still found only in whole units of e?
ex.a: Quarks are always bound into whole-charge particles.

topics.title: Coulomb's law
topics.goal: F = kq₁q₂/r².
checks: I can compute electric forces between point charges.

ex.q: Find the force between two 1 μC charges 1 m apart.
Find the force between an electron and a proton 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m apart.
Find the force between two 1 C charges 1 km apart. What does this say about the size of a coulomb?
ex.a: About 9,000 N: a coulomb is enormous.

topics.title: Conductors and insulators
topics.goal: Why charges move in some materials only.
checks: I can explain why some materials conduct and what a Faraday cage does.

ex.q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
Why are you safe inside a car struck by lightning?
ex.a: Charge stays on the outer metal

ex.q: Why do phones often lose signal in lifts?
ex.a: The metal box blocks radio waves.

topics.title: Electric fields
topics.goal: The field as force per unit charge.
checks: I can compute fields and draw field lines.

ex.q: Find the field 1 m from a 1 μC charge.
Find the field a proton makes 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m away.
Sketch the field lines of a dipole.
Why is the field between two large charged plates uniform?
ex.a: Contributions from all over the plates add evenly.

topics.title: Electric dipoles
topics.goal: Dipole moment p = qd and the torque a field puts on it.
checks: I can use p = qd and the torque p × E.

ex.q: A water molecule has a dipole moment of 6.2 × 10⁻³⁰ C·m. How far apart would charges ±e need to be to give this?
When is the torque on a dipole largest?
ex.a: When it is perpendicular to the field

ex.q: How does a microwave oven use dipoles to heat food?
ex.a: The oscillating field keeps twisting water molecules, and friction heats the food.

topics.title: Electric potential and voltage
topics.goal: Voltage is energy per charge.
checks: I can compute potentials and energy changes from voltages.

ex.q: How much energy does an electron gain crossing 1 V?
Find the potential 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m from a proton.
Why can birds sit safely on a high-voltage wire?
ex.a: No potential difference across their body.

topics.title: The electron volt
topics.goal: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; atomic energies are a few eV.
checks: I can move between eV and joules and know typical energies.

ex.q: Convert 13.6 eV to joules.
What range of photon energies is visible light, in eV?
Put in order: kT at room temperature, a visible photon, the electron's rest energy, the proton's rest energy, an LHC proton.
ex.a: 0.026 eV, about 2 eV, 511 keV, 938 MeV, 6.8 TeV.

topics.title: Capacitors
topics.goal: Storing charge and energy.
checks: I can use C = ε₀A/d and E = ½CV².

ex.q: Find the capacitance of 1 m² plates 1 mm apart.
Find the energy stored in 1 μF at 100 V.
Why does a camera flash use a capacitor?
ex.a: It releases stored energy in a burst

ex.q: Why does a capacitor block steady current?
ex.a: Once charged, no more current flows.

topics.title: Current, resistance and Ohm's law
topics.goal: V = IR.
checks: I can use V = IR, P = VI and R = ρL/A.

ex.q: A 46 Ω heater runs on 230 V. Find the current and power.
Electrons drift through a wire at about a millimetre per second, yet the light turns on instantly. Why?
ex.a: The field travels at near light speed and pushes all electrons at once

ex.q: Find the resistance of 1 m of copper wire with a 1 mm² cross-section (ρ = 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m).

topics.title: Series and parallel circuits
topics.goal: Analyze simple circuits.
checks: I can combine resistors and use Kirchhoff's laws.

ex.q: Combine 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series and in parallel.
Three 6 Ω bulbs in parallel run from 12 V. Find the total current.
A 12 V battery drives 4 Ω and 2 Ω in series. Find the current and the voltage across each.

topics.title: Where electrical energy really flows
topics.goal: Energy travels in the fields, not the wires.
checks: I can explain energy flow in circuits with the Poynting vector.

ex.q: In Veritasium's thought experiment the bulb is 1 m from the battery but the wires are light-seconds long. Roughly when does the bulb first light?
ex.a: After about 1 m/c, a few nanoseconds

ex.q: Around a wire carrying current, which way does the Poynting vector point?
ex.a: Into the wire, toward the resistor

ex.q: In a battery-and-resistor circuit, does the energy travel inside the wires or around them?

topics.title: Magnets and magnetic fields
topics.goal: Field lines and poles.
checks: I can describe magnetic fields and their typical strengths.

ex.q: What happens when you cut a bar magnet in half?
Is Earth's geographic North Pole a magnetic north or south pole?
Order by strength: Earth's field, a fridge magnet, an MRI scanner.
ex.a: Earth (50 μT), fridge magnet (millitesla), MRI (1.5 to 3 T).

topics.title: The Lorentz force
topics.search: Lorentz force charged particle in magnetic field
topics.goal: Charges circle in a magnetic field (cyclotrons, mass spectrometers).
checks: I can compute the circular motion of charges in a magnetic field.

ex.q: An electron at 10⁶ m/s moves in a 1 mT field. Find the radius of its circle (mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg).
Show the orbit frequency eB/(2πm) does not depend on speed. Evaluate it for electrons in 1 T.
Why are auroras near the poles?
ex.a: Particles spiral along field lines into the polar regions.

topics.title: The classical Hall effect
topics.goal: A sideways voltage in a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (the quantum Hall effect builds on it).
checks: I can derive the Hall voltage and use it to find carrier sign and density.

ex.q: Derive V_H = IB/(nqt) for a strip of thickness t.
How does the sign of V_H reveal whether carriers are positive or negative?
ex.a: The carriers pile up on opposite sides

ex.q: Find V_H for copper (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³) with 1 A, 1 T and t = 0.1 mm.
In the quantum Hall effect (17.56), what becomes quantized?
ex.a: The Hall resistance, in steps of h/e².

topics.title: Magnetic fields from currents
topics.search: magnetic field from a current Ampere's law
topics.goal: Currents make magnetic fields.
checks: I can compute fields of wires and solenoids.

ex.q: Find the field 1 cm from a wire carrying 10 A. Compare with Earth's 50 μT.
A solenoid has 1000 turns per metre and carries 2 A. Find the field inside.
Do parallel currents attract or repel?

topics.title: Induction
topics.search: electromagnetic induction Faraday's law Lenz's law
topics.goal: Changing magnetic fields make voltages.
checks: I can use Faraday's law and Lenz's law.

ex.q: Drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe. Why does it fall slowly?
A 100-turn coil's flux changes by 0.01 Wb in 0.1 s. Find the induced voltage.
How does an induction hob heat a pan without getting hot itself?
ex.a: Changing magnetic fields induce currents in the pan.

topics.title: Inductance
topics.goal: Coils resist changes in current; energy ½LI².
checks: I can use E = ½LI² and the LC frequency 1/√(LC).

ex.q: Find the energy in a 1 H inductor carrying 2 A.
Find the resonant frequency of 1 mH with 1 nF.
Compare an LC circuit with a mass on a spring. Which plays the mass, which the spring?
ex.a: L plays the mass, 1/C the spring constant

ex.q: Why does switching off a big inductor make a spark?
ex.a: The current cannot stop instantly, so the voltage spikes.

topics.title: Gauss's law
topics.goal: Flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge.
checks: I can use symmetry and Gauss's law to find fields.

ex.q: Derive Coulomb's law from Gauss's law.
Find the field of a large flat sheet with charge density σ.
Why is the field zero inside a closed conducting shell?
ex.a: Charges move until the inside field cancels

ex.q: Find the field inside a uniformly charged ball.

topics.title: The Biot-Savart law
topics.goal: Compute fields from currents.
checks: I can integrate Biot-Savart for simple shapes.

ex.q: Find the field at the centre of a circular loop of radius R.
Derive the field of a long straight wire.
Find the field on the axis of a loop at distance z.

topics.title: Maxwell's equations
topics.goal: All four equations in words and pictures.
checks: I can state all four equations in words and symbols.

ex.q: Write each equation in one sentence.
Which equation says there are no magnetic monopoles?
Why did Maxwell need the displacement current? Use a charging capacitor.
ex.a: Ampere's law gives different answers for surfaces that pass between the plates

ex.q: How many scalar equations are the four, written in components?

topics.title: Maxwell's equations predict light
topics.goal: Derive the wave equation and the speed of light.
checks: I can derive the wave equation and the speed of light.

ex.q: Derive the vacuum wave equation using 4.21 Exercise 3.
Compute 1/√(μ₀ε₀).
Why was this the moment optics became part of electromagnetism?
ex.a: The predicted wave speed matched the measured speed of light.

topics.title: Energy and momentum in fields
topics.search: energy in electromagnetic fields Poynting vector
topics.goal: Fields carry energy and momentum.
checks: I can use I = ½cε₀E² and radiation pressure I/c.

ex.q: Sunlight above the atmosphere is 1361 W/m². Find the peak electric field.
Find the pressure of sunlight on a black surface.
Why do comet tails point away from the Sun?
ex.a: Radiation pressure and the solar wind push dust and gas.

topics.title: Magnetic dipole moments
topics.goal: A loop of current is a tiny magnet; spin works similarly.
checks: I can compute μ = IA and the energy −μ · B.

ex.q: Find the moment of a 1 cm² loop carrying 1 A.
An electron orbits with angular momentum ħ. Show its magnetic moment is eħ/(2m) and evaluate this Bohr magneton (ħ = 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴).
Find the energy of one Bohr magneton in 1 T, in eV.

topics.title: Forces on dipoles
topics.search: force on a magnetic dipole in a non-uniform field
topics.goal: Needed to understand the Stern-Gerlach experiment.
checks: I can explain why only a non-uniform field pushes a dipole.

ex.q: Show the force on a dipole along z is μ_z dB/dz.
A silver atom (1.8 × 10⁻²⁵ kg) with one Bohr magneton sits in a 10 T/m gradient. Find its acceleration.
Why does a uniform field only twist a dipole?
ex.a: The forces on its two ends cancel.

topics.title: Types of magnetism
topics.goal: Three kinds of magnetism (all quantum in origin).
checks: I can tell diamagnetism, paramagnetism and ferromagnetism apart.

ex.q: Classify water, liquid oxygen and iron.
How was a live frog levitated in a 16 T magnet?
What happens to iron above 770 °C?
Classical physics predicts no magnetism at all (17.38). Write down why that should surprise you.

topics.title: Dielectrics
topics.goal: How matter responds to fields.
checks: I can explain how a dielectric weakens fields.

ex.q: Water has κ ≈ 80. What happens to a capacitor filled with water?
Use κ to explain why water dissolves salt.
ex.a: Ions attract 80 times more weakly in water

ex.q: What is dielectric breakdown? Give an example.
ex.a: The insulator fails and conducts, as in lightning.

topics.title: Scalar and vector potentials
topics.goal: E and B from φ and A (needed for the Aharonov-Bohm effect).
checks: I can get E and B from φ and A.

ex.q: Write E and B in terms of φ and A.
Check that A = (−By/2, Bx/2, 0) gives a uniform field B along z.
Outside a long solenoid B = 0. Is A zero there too? (See 19.25.)

topics.title: Gauge invariance
topics.goal: Different potentials give the same fields.
checks: I can show that a gauge change leaves the fields unchanged.

ex.q: Show that A → A + ∇χ and φ → φ − ∂χ/∂t leave E and B unchanged.
In quantum mechanics the wavefunction also changes by a phase. Which phase? (See 20.21.)

topics.title: Radiation from accelerating charges
topics.search: radiation from accelerating charges Larmor formula
topics.goal: Why a classical orbiting electron would spiral into the nucleus.
checks: I can use the Larmor formula and explain the classical atom problem.

ex.q: Write the Larmor formula.
Classically, an orbiting electron radiates away its energy in about 10⁻¹¹ s. Explain the logic (see 14.4).
How do synchrotron light sources use this effect?
ex.a: Electrons forced around a ring emit intense X-rays.

topics.title: Magnetism from relativity
topics.search: how special relativity makes magnets work Veritasium
topics.goal: Magnetism as electricity seen from another frame.
checks: I can explain magnetism as electricity seen from another frame.

ex.q: A charge moves beside a current-carrying wire. Explain the force in the charge's own frame.
ex.a: In its frame, length contraction makes the wire's charges unbalance

ex.q: Why is a tiny relativistic effect strong enough to drive motors?
ex.a: Wires hold about 10²³ electrons per cm³

ex.q: Do E and B mix when you change frames?

topics.title: AC and transformers
topics.goal: Alternating current basics.
checks: I can work with rms values and transformer ratios.

ex.q: What is the peak of 230 V rms?
A transformer turns 230 V into 12 V. What turns ratio does it need?
Why do power lines use very high voltage?
ex.a: Lower current means lower I²R losses.

topics.title: Plasma basics
topics.goal: The fourth state of matter.
checks: I can describe plasma and name examples.

ex.q: Name four plasmas on Earth or in space.
ex.a: The Sun, lightning, neon signs, fusion reactors

ex.q: Why does the ionosphere reflect some radio waves but let light through?
ex.a: Waves below the plasma frequency reflect

ex.q: What is Debye shielding?
ex.a: Free charges screen fields beyond a short distance.

topics.title: The multipole expansion
topics.goal: Monopole, dipole, quadrupole.
checks: I can say how monopole, dipole and quadrupole potentials fall off.

ex.q: How do the potentials of a monopole, dipole and quadrupole fall with distance?
Why does a neutral molecule still feel electric forces?
Link this to the Legendre expansion in 5.22.

topics.title: The electromagnetic Lagrangian
topics.goal: Maxwell's equations from a Lagrangian (bridge to QFT).
checks: I can derive the Lorentz force from a Lagrangian.

ex.q: Use L = ½mv² − qφ + qv · A to derive the Lorentz force.
Show the canonical momentum is p = mv + qA. Why does quantum mechanics replace p with p − qA?
ex.a: The momentum in the Schrödinger equation must include the field

ex.q: Which field equations come from the Lagrangian density −¼F_μνF^μν?

topics.title: A full electromagnetism course
topics.search: MIT 8.02 Walter Lewin electricity and magnetism
topics.goal: A full lecture course with live demonstrations.
checks: I can solve mixed circuit and field problems.

ex.q: A 2 μF capacitor at 10 V discharges through 1 kΩ. Find the time constant and the energy released.
A metal rod slides on rails 0.5 m apart at 2 m/s through 0.4 T. Find the induced voltage.

parts.name: Relativity
parts.title: Special and general relativity
parts.intro: Use c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s and γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). Highlight: in 12.15 the rapidity for 0.6c turns out to be exactly ln 2.

topics.title: The Michelson-Morley experiment
topics.goal: No ether: light's speed does not depend on the observer.
checks: I can explain what the experiment expected and what it found.

ex.q: If light moved through an ether and Earth moved through that ether, why would the two arms disagree?
ex.a: Light would move at different speeds along and across the motion

ex.q: What did the null result mean?
ex.a: There is no detectable ether; light's speed is the same

ex.q: Modern versions test the constancy of light's speed to about 1 part in 10¹⁷. Why keep testing?
ex.a: Any tiny violation would point to new physics.

topics.title: The postulates
topics.goal: Same laws in every inertial frame; same speed of light.
checks: I can state both postulates and their first consequence.

ex.q: State the two postulates.
ex.a: Physics is the same in every inertial frame; light's speed is the same for all observers

ex.q: At 16, Einstein imagined riding alongside a light beam. Why does the second postulate forbid what he would see?
ex.a: He would see frozen light, impossible if light always moves at c

ex.q: Why must simultaneity become relative?
ex.a: Different observers disagree on which distant events happen together.

topics.title: Spacetime diagrams
topics.search: minutephysics introduction to special relativity spacetime diagrams
topics.goal: Read spacetime diagrams.
checks: I can draw worldlines and a moving observer's axes.

ex.q: Draw worldlines for an object at rest, one moving at 0.5c, and a light pulse.
Why can no worldline be flatter than 45°?
ex.a: That would be faster than light.

ex.q: Draw the time and space axes of an observer moving at 0.5c.

topics.title: Time dilation
topics.goal: Moving clocks run slow by γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).
checks: I can derive time dilation from a light clock and compute γ.

ex.q: Find γ at 0.6c, 0.8c and 0.99c.
Derive γ from a light clock bouncing between two mirrors.
A ship flies to a star 4 light-years away at 0.8c. How long does the trip take for Earth and for the crew?
GPS satellites move at 3.9 km/s. By how many microseconds per day do their clocks fall behind from speed alone?

topics.title: Length contraction
topics.goal: Moving objects shrink along their motion.
checks: I can compute contracted lengths and resolve the pole-and-barn paradox.

ex.q: A 100 m ship flies at 0.6c. How long does it look from Earth?
A 10 m pole flies through a 8 m barn at 0.6c. From the barn it fits; from the pole the barn is even shorter. Who is right?
ex.a: Both: they disagree on whether the doors close simultaneously

ex.q: Describe muon survival (12.8) from the muon's point of view.
ex.a: The atmosphere is contracted, so the trip is short.

topics.title: Relativity of simultaneity
topics.goal: "At the same time" depends on the observer.
checks: I can tell when two events can look simultaneous to someone.

ex.q: Lightning hits both ends of a moving train at the same moment for the platform. What does someone in the middle of the train see?
Two events are 1 μs and 1 km apart. Can some observer see them as simultaneous?
ex.a: Yes: 1 km > 300 m, so the separation is spacelike

ex.q: Can the order of cause and effect ever flip?

topics.title: The twin paradox
topics.goal: Why the travelling twin is younger.
checks: I can explain why the travelling twin ages less.

ex.q: Why is the situation not symmetric?
ex.a: Only the traveller turns around and changes frames

ex.q: For the round trip in 12.4 Exercise 3, how much does each twin age?
Look up the Hafele-Keating experiment. What did the atomic clocks on planes show?
ex.a: Eastward clocks lost and westward clocks gained time, as predicted.

topics.title: Muons prove time dilation
topics.goal: Real evidence for time dilation.
checks: I can compute how far a fast muon travels.

ex.q: A muon lives 2.2 μs at rest and moves at 0.998c. How far would it go without time dilation? With it?
Why do so many muons reach sea level?
ex.a: Their clocks run slow by γ.

topics.title: The Lorentz transformation
topics.goal: Transform coordinates between frames.
checks: I can transform events between frames and show x² − c²t² is invariant.

ex.q: An event is at x = 1 m, t = 0. Find t′ in a frame moving at 0.6c.
Show x² − c²t² is the same in both frames.
Show the transformation becomes Galilean when v ≪ c.

topics.title: Relativistic velocity addition
topics.goal: Why adding speeds never gives more than c.
checks: I can add velocities with (u + v)/(1 + uv/c²).

ex.q: A rocket at 0.6c fires a probe forward at 0.6c. How fast is the probe relative to Earth?
Add c to any speed v. What do you get?
Look up the Fizeau experiment with light in flowing water. What did it measure?
ex.a: Light is dragged less than simple addition predicts, matching relativity.

topics.title: The spacetime interval
topics.goal: The invariant interval; causality.
checks: I can classify intervals and compute proper time.

ex.q: Classify two events 1 s and 1 light-year apart.
A clock moves at 0.6c for 10 s of Earth time. How much proper time does it record?
Label the regions of a light cone. Which can influence you now?
ex.a: Past cone, future cone, elsewhere; only the past cone.

topics.title: Four-vectors
topics.goal: Energy and momentum as one 4-vector.
checks: I can use four-momentum and its invariant.

ex.q: Write the four-momentum of a particle.
Show its invariant is m²c² (or E² − p²c² = m²c⁴).
Show every four-velocity has the same magnitude.

topics.title: E = mc²
topics.goal: Mass is a form of energy.
checks: I can convert mass to energy and back.

ex.q: How much energy is in 1 g of mass? Compare with a 15 kiloton bomb (6.3 × 10¹³ J).
The Sun loses about 4.3 million tonnes of mass per second. What power does it radiate?
A hydrogen atom weighs less than a separate proton and electron. By how much, in kg? (Binding energy 13.6 eV.)

topics.title: The energy-momentum relation
topics.goal: Massless photons still carry momentum p = E/c.
checks: I can use E² = (pc)² + (mc²)².

ex.q: Find the momentum of a 2 eV photon in kg·m/s.
An electron has 1 MeV of kinetic energy. Find its total energy and pc in MeV.
Show that a massless particle must move at c.
ex.a: With m = 0, E = pc, so v = pc²/E = c.

topics.title: The relativistic Doppler effect
topics.goal: Redshift from motion.
checks: I can compute relativistic frequency shifts.

ex.q: A source recedes at 0.6c. By what factor is its frequency lowered?
A redshift z = 1 means the wavelength doubled. What recession speed is that in special relativity? (Cosmology changes this, 12.28.)
Why is there a shift even for motion straight across your line of sight?

topics.title: Rapidity
topics.search: rapidity and hyperbolic geometry of spacetime
topics.goal: Boosts as hyperbolic rotations.
checks: I can convert between speed and rapidity and add rapidities.

ex.q: Find the rapidity of 0.6c from tanh η = v/c.
Redo 12.9b Exercise 1 by adding rapidities.
A rocket accelerates at 1 g (as felt by its crew) for one year of crew time. Its rapidity is gτ/c. What speed does it reach?

topics.title: The equivalence principle
topics.goal: Gravity and acceleration are locally indistinguishable.
checks: I can explain why gravity and acceleration look the same locally.

ex.q: In a closed lift, can you tell whether you are on Earth or accelerating at 1 g in space?
A light beam crosses an accelerating lift. Why does it bend, and what does this predict for gravity?
ex.a: The floor rises while the beam crosses: gravity should bend light

ex.q: Why did the hammer and feather on the Moon fall together?

topics.title: Gravity as curved spacetime
topics.search: why gravity is not a force Veritasium
topics.goal: Free fall is natural motion through curved spacetime.
checks: I can explain why free fall is natural motion.

ex.q: Why do you feel weightless when falling?
ex.a: You follow a straight path in spacetime

ex.q: In what sense is the ground pushing you upward right now?
ex.a: It stops you following your free-fall path

ex.q: Two people walk due north from different points on the equator and get closer. Is a force pulling them together?

topics.title: Gravitational time dilation
topics.goal: Clocks run slower deeper in gravity; GPS corrects for it.
checks: I can estimate gravitational clock shifts with gh/c².

ex.q: GPS clocks gain about 45 μs/day from gravity and lose about 7 from speed. What is the net effect, and what happens if it is ignored?
ex.a: +38 μs/day; positions drift by about 10 km a day

ex.q: Find the fractional rate change between clocks 1 m apart in height.
In the film Interstellar, why does an hour on Miller's planet equal years on Earth?
ex.a: It orbits deep in a black hole's gravity.

topics.title: Visualizing general relativity
topics.goal: Visual intuition for curved spacetime.
checks: I can explain why curved time, not just curved space, makes things fall.

ex.q: Explain why a ball dropped from rest starts to fall if only time is warped.
ex.a: Its path through warped time tilts it toward slower-clock regions

ex.q: What is misleading about the rubber-sheet picture?
ex.a: It uses gravity to explain gravity and hides curved time.

topics.title: The metric tensor
topics.goal: How the metric measures distances in spacetime.
checks: I can read distances from a metric.

ex.q: Write the Minkowski metric.
Write the metric of a sphere of radius R.
Use it to find the distance along the equator between longitudes 0° and 90°.

topics.title: Geodesics
topics.goal: Paths of free-falling objects.
checks: I can explain orbits and light bending as geodesics.

ex.q: Why do flights from Europe to the US curve over Greenland on a flat map?
ex.a: Great circles are shortest on a sphere

ex.q: In what sense is the Moon's orbit a straight line?
ex.a: It is a geodesic in curved spacetime

ex.q: Eddington measured starlight bending by 1.75″ at the Sun's edge in 1919. Why was that the decisive test?

topics.title: The Riemann curvature tensor
topics.goal: How curvature is measured.
checks: I can link curvature to tidal forces.

ex.q: How many independent components does the Riemann tensor have in 4D?
Why do tides show spacetime curvature better than ordinary gravity does?
ex.a: Uniform gravity can be removed by falling; tides cannot

ex.q: What is spaghettification?

topics.title: Einstein's field equations
topics.goal: Matter tells spacetime how to curve.
checks: I can read the equations in words.

ex.q: How many independent equations are in G_μν = 8πGT_μν/c⁴?
Why does the tiny factor 8πG/c⁴ mean spacetime is very stiff?
What does the cosmological constant term do?
ex.a: Gives empty space an energy that drives expansion.

topics.title: Black holes and the Schwarzschild metric
topics.goal: The spacetime outside a black hole; event horizon.
checks: I can compute Schwarzschild radii and name the special radii.

ex.q: Find the Schwarzschild radius of the Sun.
Sagittarius A* has about 4 million solar masses. Find its radius in km and in AU (1 AU = 1.5 × 10⁸ km).
At what radius can light orbit a black hole?

topics.title: Penrose diagrams
topics.goal: Map infinite spacetimes on a page.
checks: I can read a Penrose diagram.

ex.q: Draw the Penrose diagram of flat spacetime and label infinity.
Draw a Schwarzschild black hole. Why must every path inside the horizon end at the singularity?
ex.a: Inside, the singularity lies in every future direction.

topics.title: Gravitational waves
topics.goal: Ripples of spacetime and how they were detected.
checks: I can explain how LIGO detects strains of 10⁻²¹.

ex.q: A strain of 10⁻²¹ on a 4 km arm changes its length by how much?
The first event, GW150914, radiated about 3 solar masses of energy in a fraction of a second. How many joules is that?
Why does the signal "chirp" upward in frequency?
ex.a: The orbit shrinks and speeds up.

topics.title: Rotating black holes
topics.goal: Frame dragging.
checks: I can describe frame dragging and the ergosphere.

ex.q: What is the ergosphere, and how can the Penrose process extract energy?
ex.a: A region where nothing can stay still; objects can leave with more energy than they entered

ex.q: Which satellite measured frame dragging around Earth?

topics.title: The expanding universe
topics.goal: Galaxies recede faster the farther they are.
checks: I can use Hubble's law and estimate the age of the universe.

ex.q: With H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc, how fast does a galaxy 100 Mpc away recede?
Estimate the Hubble time 1/H₀ in years (1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10¹⁹ km).
Why can distant galaxies recede faster than light without breaking relativity?

topics.title: The Friedmann equations
topics.goal: How the universe's expansion depends on its contents.
checks: I can describe how matter, radiation and dark energy shape expansion.

ex.q: How does the scale factor grow in a matter-only and in a radiation-only universe?
Find the critical density 3H²/(8πG) for H₀ = 70 km/s/Mpc. How many protons per cubic metre is that?
ex.a: About 9 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/m³, about 5 protons per m³

ex.q: What makes the expansion accelerate?

topics.title: The cosmic microwave background
topics.goal: Light left over from 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
checks: I can explain where the CMB came from and what its ripples mean.

ex.q: The CMB was released at redshift about 1100. How hot was it then?
Why is it microwaves today? (Use 10.13b Exercise 4.)
ex.a: Its 2.7 K blackbody peaks near 1 mm

ex.q: Its temperature varies by about 1 part in 100,000. What do those ripples become? (See 22.22.)

topics.title: Dark matter and dark energy
topics.search: dark matter and dark energy evidence
topics.goal: What we know and do not know.
checks: I can give the main evidence for each.

ex.q: What do galaxy rotation curves show?
ex.a: Stars far out orbit too fast for the visible mass

ex.q: Why is the Bullet Cluster strong evidence for dark matter?
ex.a: Its mass (from lensing) is separated from its hot gas

ex.q: Roughly what fractions of the universe are ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy?

topics.title: Full relativity courses
topics.search: Susskind Theoretical Minimum special relativity and general relativity
topics.goal: Full lecture courses on both theories.
checks: I can solve mixed problems in special and general relativity.

ex.q: An electron is accelerated through 1 million volts. Find γ and its speed.
A clock sits on a mountain 3 km high for a year. How much does it gain on a clock at sea level?

parts.name: Chemistry
parts.title: Chemistry
parts.intro: Highlight: in 13.34 a particle-in-a-box estimate predicts the colour a molecule absorbs to within a few percent, and in 13.44 relativity explains why gold is gold.

topics.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
topics.goal: Tell the three apart.
checks: I can classify substances and separate simple mixtures.

ex.q: Classify: air, water, gold, salt water, carbon dioxide.
How would you separate salt from sand?

topics.title: History of the atom
topics.search: history of the atom Dalton Thomson Rutherford Bohr
topics.goal: How the picture of the atom changed.
checks: I can put the atomic models in order and say what each fixed.

ex.q: Order Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr and give each model in one line.
ex.a: Solid spheres; plum pudding; tiny nucleus; quantized orbits

ex.q: Which experiment killed the plum-pudding model?

topics.title: Protons, neutrons and electrons
topics.search: protons neutrons electrons atomic number mass number
topics.goal: Read an element's symbol, Z and A.
checks: I can read Z and A and count particles in atoms and ions.

ex.q: Count protons, neutrons and electrons in carbon-14.
Count them in uranium-238.
Count them in the ion ²³Na⁺.

topics.title: Isotopes
topics.goal: Same element, different neutron count (helium-3 vs helium-4).
checks: I can explain isotopes and average atomic masses.

ex.q: Count the protons and neutrons in helium-3 and helium-4. Which is a boson? (Use 17.13.)
Chlorine is a mix of ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl with average mass 35.45. What fraction is ³⁵Cl?
Why do isotopes behave almost the same chemically?

topics.title: The mole
topics.goal: 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
checks: I can convert between grams, moles and particles.

ex.q: How many molecules are in 18 g of water?
How many moles of water are in 1 kg?
What is the mass of one carbon-12 atom in grams?

topics.title: The periodic table and its trends
topics.goal: Groups, periods and trends in size and reactivity.
checks: I can predict size and reactivity trends.

ex.q: How does atomic radius change across a period and down a group? Why?
ex.a: Shrinks across (more nuclear charge), grows down (more shells)

ex.q: Why are the group 1 metals so reactive?
Why are noble gases so unreactive?

topics.title: Element by element
topics.goal: An element-by-element channel; start with helium.
checks: I can tell a story about at least five elements.

ex.q: Helium makes your voice sound squeaky. Sound travels about 2.8 times faster in helium. Is your vocal cords' pitch changing, or something else?
ex.a: The pitch barely changes; the vocal tract's resonances shift up.

ex.q: Watch five Periodic Videos and write one surprising fact for each element.

topics.title: Valence electrons
topics.goal: Valence electrons decide chemistry.
checks: I can count valence electrons and predict bonding.

ex.q: Give the valence electrons of C, O, Na, Cl and Ne.
Why does oxygen usually form two bonds?
ex.a: It needs two more electrons to fill its shell.

topics.title: Electron configurations
topics.search: electron configuration s p d f orbitals
topics.goal: Write configurations like 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.
checks: I can write configurations, including known exceptions.

ex.q: Write the configurations of N, Fe and Cu.
How many electrons fit in shell n? Check for n = 1, 2, 3.
How many orbitals make up a d subshell?

topics.title: Aufbau, Hund and Pauli
topics.search: Aufbau principle Hund's rule Pauli exclusion
topics.goal: Fill orbitals correctly (all three rules are quantum).
checks: I can fill orbital boxes correctly and name the rule behind each step.

ex.q: Draw the 2p boxes for carbon, nitrogen and oxygen.
ex.a: C: two unpaired; N: three unpaired; O: one pair and two unpaired

ex.q: Why can't two electrons in the same orbital have the same spin?
How many unpaired electrons does an oxygen atom have?

topics.title: Ionization energy
topics.goal: Energy to remove or add an electron.
checks: I can explain ionization energy trends and jumps.

ex.q: Why does helium have the highest ionization energy (24.6 eV)?
ex.a: Two electrons close to a charge-2 nucleus in a full shell

ex.q: Hydrogen's ionization energy is 13.6 eV. Where will you derive this number? (See 14.9 and 4.20.)
Why is sodium's second ionization energy so much bigger than its first?
ex.a: The second comes from a full inner shell.

topics.title: Electronegativity
topics.goal: Which atom pulls electrons harder.
checks: I can predict bond polarity from electronegativity.

ex.q: Order F, O, N and C by electronegativity.
Which end of H–Cl is slightly negative?

topics.title: Ionic bonding
topics.goal: Electron transfer and lattices.
checks: I can explain ionic lattices and their properties.

ex.q: Describe the NaCl lattice.
ex.a: Alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in a cube

ex.q: Why are ionic solids brittle, and why do they conduct only when melted or dissolved?
ex.a: Shifting layers lines up like charges; ions must move to conduct

ex.q: Why is MgO's lattice far stronger than NaCl's?

topics.title: Covalent bonding
topics.goal: Electron sharing.
checks: I can describe single, double and triple bonds.

ex.q: The H–H bond energy is 436 kJ/mol. Convert it to eV per bond.
What kind of bond holds N₂ together?
Why is diamond so hard?

topics.title: Metallic bonding
topics.goal: A sea of electrons.
checks: I can explain metals' shine and malleability.

ex.q: Why are metals shiny?
Why can metals be hammered flat without shattering?
ex.a: The electron sea lets atoms slide.

topics.title: Lewis structures
topics.goal: Draw molecules with lone pairs and bonds.
checks: I can draw Lewis structures with formal charges and resonance.

ex.q: Draw H₂O, CO₂, NH₃ and N₂.
Find the formal charges in CO.
ex.a: Formally C is −1 and O is +1 in the triple-bonded structure.

ex.q: Draw the two resonance structures of ozone.

topics.title: VSEPR shapes
topics.goal: Predict molecular shapes.
checks: I can predict molecular shapes and angles.

ex.q: Give the shapes and angles of CH₄, NH₃, H₂O and CO₂.
Why do lone pairs squeeze bond angles?

topics.title: Polarity
topics.goal: Dipoles from uneven sharing.
checks: I can tell polar from non-polar molecules.

ex.q: Which are polar: CO₂, H₂O, CCl₄, NH₃?
Why don't oil and water mix?
ex.a: Water's hydrogen bonds hold it together and exclude non-polar oil.

topics.title: Intermolecular forces
topics.search: intermolecular forces hydrogen bonding London dispersion
topics.goal: Forces between molecules (London forces are a quantum effect).
checks: I can rank intermolecular forces and explain London forces.

ex.q: Order by boiling point: CH₄, H₂O, HF.
How do geckos stick to walls?
ex.a: Van der Waals forces from millions of tiny hairs.

ex.q: Explain London dispersion forces as electron clouds fluctuating together.

topics.title: Balancing equations
topics.goal: Conserve atoms in reactions.
checks: I can balance any simple reaction.

ex.q: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃
C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

topics.title: Stoichiometry
topics.goal: Calculate amounts in reactions.
checks: I can compute amounts and limiting reagents.

ex.q: How many grams of CO₂ come from burning 16 g of methane?
Mix 4 g of H₂ with 32 g of O₂ and react them fully. What forms, how much, and is anything left?

topics.title: Molarity and dilution
topics.goal: Concentration in mol/L and dilution.
checks: I can work with mol/L and dilute solutions.

ex.q: 58.5 g of NaCl is dissolved to make 1 L. What is the molarity?
Dilute 100 mL of 2 M solution to 500 mL. What is the new molarity?
How many ions are in 1 L of 1 M NaCl?

topics.title: Acids and bases
topics.goal: Proton transfer and the pH scale.
checks: I can compute pH for strong acids and bases.

ex.q: Find the pH of 0.01 M HCl.
Find the pH of 0.001 M NaOH.
Why is pH 7 neutral at 25 °C?

topics.title: Redox reactions
topics.goal: Electron transfer reactions.
checks: I can identify what is oxidized and what is reduced.

ex.q: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which is oxidized?
In a battery, which electrode is oxidized?
Describe rusting as a redox reaction.

topics.title: Reaction rates and activation energy
topics.goal: Energy barriers to reactions (quantum tunneling can bypass them).
checks: I can use the Arrhenius factor e^(−Eₐ/kT).

ex.q: A reaction has Eₐ = 0.5 eV. By what factor does its rate rise from 300 K to 310 K?
ex.a: About 1.9: the old rule that rates double every 10 K

ex.q: What does a catalyst change?
How could quantum tunneling let a reaction go faster than Arrhenius predicts? (See 24.14.)

topics.title: Chemical equilibrium
topics.goal: Reversible reactions balance.
checks: I can write K and use Le Chatelier's principle.

ex.q: Write K for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.
The reaction releases heat. What does heating do to the yield?
Why does the Haber process use high pressure?
ex.a: Fewer gas molecules on the product side.

topics.title: Enthalpy and Hess's law
topics.goal: Heat of reaction.
checks: I can combine reactions and use bond energies.

ex.q: C + O₂ → CO₂ releases 394 kJ/mol and CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ releases 283 kJ/mol. Find the heat released by C + ½O₂ → CO.
Estimate the energy change of H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl from bond energies 436, 243 and 431 kJ/mol.

topics.title: Gibbs free energy
topics.goal: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
checks: I can predict spontaneity with ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

ex.q: For ammonia synthesis ΔH = −92 kJ and ΔS = −199 J/K. Find ΔG at 298 K and 500 K. Above what temperature does it stop being spontaneous?
ex.a: About −33 kJ; about +7.5 kJ; about 462 K

ex.q: Ammonium nitrate dissolving absorbs heat (cold packs). Why does it happen anyway?

topics.title: Emission spectra
topics.goal: Each element emits its own colors.
checks: I can link flame colours to energy levels.

ex.q: Match flame colours: sodium, copper, strontium, potassium.
Sodium's yellow line is 589 nm. What energy gap is that in eV?
Why does each element have its own spectrum?

topics.title: Why things have colour
topics.goal: Color from electrons jumping between levels.
checks: I can explain colour as the light that is not absorbed.

ex.q: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue. Why are leaves green?
β-carotene absorbs blue. What colour are carrots?
Predict whether a longer chain of alternating bonds absorbs longer or shorter wavelengths. (Check in 13.34.)

topics.title: The Beer-Lambert law
topics.goal: Absorbance grows with concentration and path length.
checks: I can use A = εlc and convert absorbance to transmission.

ex.q: A sample has absorbance 1. What fraction of light passes?
Double the concentration. What fraction passes now?
Make tea of different strengths, photograph them against a white phone screen, and check that the colour depth grows with concentration.

topics.title: Fluorescence and phosphorescence
topics.goal: Delayed light emission and why it differs.
checks: I can explain why emitted light is redder and why some glow lasts.

ex.q: Why does tonic water glow blue under UV light?
Why is fluorescent light always at a longer wavelength than the light that excites it?
ex.a: Some energy is lost as vibration first

ex.q: Why does phosphorescence last so long? (Hint: a spin must flip.)

topics.title: Hybridization
topics.goal: Mixing orbitals to explain shapes.
checks: I can assign sp, sp² and sp³ and the matching angles.

ex.q: Give the hybridization of carbon in CH₄, C₂H₄ and C₂H₂.
Why is benzene flat?

topics.title: Molecular orbital theory
topics.goal: Atomic orbitals combine into molecular orbitals.
checks: I can fill MO diagrams and compute bond orders.

ex.q: Find the bond orders of H₂ and He₂. Why doesn't He₂ exist?
Find the bond order of N₂.
Find the bond order of O₂ and its number of unpaired electrons.

topics.title: Why oxygen is magnetic
topics.search: why oxygen is paramagnetic liquid oxygen magnet
topics.goal: Molecular orbitals predict that O₂ is magnetic.
checks: I can explain O₂'s paramagnetism with molecular orbitals.

ex.q: Which orbitals hold O₂'s two unpaired electrons?
Watch liquid oxygen stick between magnet poles. Why does liquid nitrogen pour straight through?
Why does the Lewis structure of O₂ fail here?

topics.title: Conjugated molecules as boxes
topics.goal: Electrons spread over a whole molecule (particle-in-a-box chemistry).
checks: I can estimate absorption colours with the particle-in-a-box model.

ex.q: Butadiene's 4 π electrons sit in a box about 0.58 nm long, filling levels 1 and 2. Energy levels are n²h²/(8mL²). Find the 2 → 3 energy and wavelength. (Measured: 217 nm.)
Use the model to explain why carrots (long chains) are coloured but butadiene is colourless.
ex.a: Longer boxes have smaller gaps, shifting absorption into visible light.

topics.title: Infrared spectroscopy
topics.goal: Bonds vibrate at quantized frequencies.
checks: I can explain why only some molecules absorb infrared.

ex.q: Why do CO₂ and H₂O absorb infrared while N₂ and O₂ do not?
Explain the greenhouse effect with this.
A C=O stretch appears at 1700 cm⁻¹. What wavelength is that?

topics.title: NMR
topics.goal: Nuclear spin flips reveal structure (the basis of MRI).
checks: I can explain NMR with spin precession.

ex.q: Protons precess at 42.58 MHz per tesla. What frequency does a 3 T MRI use?
What is a chemical shift?
ex.a: A small frequency shift from the chemical surroundings

ex.q: Which nuclei make the MRI image of your body?
ex.a: Hydrogen nuclei in water and fat.

topics.title: Crystal structures
topics.goal: Lattices like FCC and BCC.
checks: I can count atoms per unit cell.

ex.q: How many atoms are in a simple cubic, BCC and FCC unit cell?
FCC fills 74% of space. Why can't spheres do better?

topics.title: Allotropes of carbon
topics.search: allotropes of carbon diamond graphite graphene
topics.goal: Same atoms, different bonding.
checks: I can link carbon's forms to its bonding.

ex.q: Why is diamond hard and graphite soft?
ex.a: Diamond is a 3D network; graphite's layers slide

ex.q: Why does graphite conduct but diamond does not?
How was graphene first made?
ex.a: By peeling graphite with sticky tape.

topics.title: Radioactivity
topics.goal: Three types of radiation.
checks: I can write simple decay equations and know what stops each radiation.

ex.q: What stops alpha, beta and gamma radiation?
ex.a: Paper; a few mm of aluminium; thick lead

ex.q: Uranium-238 emits an alpha particle. What does it become?
Carbon-14 emits a beta particle. What does it become?

topics.title: Half-life
topics.goal: Exponential decay of nuclei.
checks: I can use half-lives for dating and safety.

ex.q: Iodine-131 has an 8-day half-life. What fraction remains after 24 days?
A bone has 25% of its original carbon-14. How old is it?

topics.title: Fission and fusion
topics.goal: Energy from splitting and joining nuclei.
checks: I can compare nuclear and chemical energies.

ex.q: One uranium-235 fission releases about 200 MeV. Burning one methane molecule releases about 9 eV. What is the ratio?
D + T → ⁴He + n releases 17.6 MeV. Where does the energy come from?
Why can both splitting heavy nuclei and joining light ones release energy? (See 21.10.)
ex.a: Iron-56 sits at the top of the binding curve.

topics.title: Organic chemistry basics
topics.goal: Carbon chemistry for the biology part.
checks: I can name common functional groups.

ex.q: Name the functional groups in ethanol, acetic acid and acetone.
How many structures can C₄H₁₀ have?

topics.title: Chirality
topics.goal: Left- and right-handed molecules.
checks: I can explain chirality and why it matters in drugs.

ex.q: What happened with thalidomide, and what does it say about mirror-image molecules?
ex.a: One mirror form treated nausea; the other caused birth defects

ex.q: How does a polarimeter tell mirror-image molecules apart?
ex.a: They rotate polarized light in opposite directions.

topics.title: Why gold is yellow
topics.goal: Relativistic effects on gold's electrons give its color.
checks: I can explain relativistic effects in heavy atoms.

ex.q: Inner electrons in an atom of charge Z move at roughly Z/137 of the speed of light. Estimate this speed and γ for gold (Z = 79).
How does this shrink gold's 6s orbital and change the colour it absorbs?
ex.a: Contraction shrinks the 5d to 6s gap, so blue light is absorbed

ex.q: Why isn't silver (Z = 47) yellow?
ex.a: Its effect is smaller and its gap stays in the UV.

topics.title: Why mercury is liquid
topics.search: why mercury is liquid relativistic effects
topics.goal: Relativity explains mercury's low melting point.
checks: I can explain mercury's low melting point with relativity.

ex.q: Why do mercury atoms hold their 6s electrons so tightly that they bond weakly?
Calculations suggest about 80% of a car battery's 2.1 V comes from relativistic effects in lead. Why would heavy elements make this possible?

topics.title: Hartree-Fock
topics.goal: Approximate many-electron atoms and molecules.
checks: I can explain the mean-field approximation for electrons.

ex.q: What does each electron "feel" in Hartree-Fock?
ex.a: The average field of the others

ex.q: What is correlation energy, and why does Hartree-Fock miss it?
ex.a: Electrons dodge each other; an average misses that

ex.q: Why must the many-electron wavefunction be a Slater determinant? (See 17.10.)

topics.title: Density functional theory
topics.goal: The workhorse of computational chemistry.
checks: I can explain the key idea behind DFT.

ex.q: What does the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem say?
Why is DFT so widely used in materials science?

topics.title: Quantum chemistry on quantum computers
topics.goal: Why molecule simulation is a key quantum computing goal.
checks: I can explain why molecules are hard to simulate.

ex.q: Why does the cost of an exact simulation grow exponentially with the number of electrons? (See 1.15b.)
ex.a: The wavefunction needs exponentially many numbers

ex.q: Why is the FeMoco cluster of nitrogenase a famous target?
ex.a: It turns nitrogen into ammonia at room temperature.

topics.title: A full chemistry course
topics.goal: A full course to fill gaps.
checks: I can do mixed chemistry problems.

ex.q: Burn 1 mol of propane. How many grams of CO₂ form?
Write the configuration of Cl⁻.
Predict the shape of SF₆.

parts.name: Key Experiments
parts.title: The experiments that broke classical physics
parts.intro: Use hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm. Highlight: in 14.3b Moseley's simple rule predicts copper's X-ray energy to within 1%.

topics.title: Discovering the electron
topics.search: Thomson cathode ray experiment discovery of the electron
topics.goal: Atoms contain smaller charged particles.
checks: I can explain how Thomson measured e/m and what it showed.

ex.q: Thomson found e/m about 1800 times larger than for hydrogen ions. What did that imply about the electron's mass?
ex.a: It is far lighter than an atom

ex.q: The electron's e/m is 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg and the proton's 9.58 × 10⁷ C/kg. Find their mass ratio.
Which everyday device used cathode rays for decades?

topics.title: Millikan's oil drops
topics.goal: Electric charge comes in fixed units.
checks: I can find the unit of charge from a set of measurements.

ex.q: Drops carry 3.2, 4.8, 8.0 and 6.4 (× 10⁻¹⁹ C). What is the smallest unit that fits all of them?
A drop of mass 10⁻¹⁵ kg floats in a field of 3.06 × 10⁴ V/m. How many electrons does it carry?
Look up the debate over how Millikan chose his data. What does it teach about honest science?

topics.title: Discovering radioactivity
topics.search: discovery of radioactivity Becquerel Marie Curie
topics.goal: Atoms are not unchangeable; some emit radiation by themselves.
checks: I can tell the story of Becquerel and the Curies.

ex.q: How did Becquerel discover radioactivity by accident?
ex.a: Uranium salts fogged wrapped photographic plates without sunlight

ex.q: Which elements did Marie and Pierre Curie discover?
Why did radioactivity show that atoms are not eternal and unchangeable?

topics.title: Rutherford's gold foil
topics.goal: The atom has a tiny dense nucleus.
checks: I can explain how the experiment revealed the nucleus.

ex.q: Why did most alpha particles pass straight through?
Why did the few that bounced back astonish Rutherford?
ex.a: They needed a tiny, dense, charged centre

ex.q: A 5 MeV alpha particle (charge 2e) heads straight at a gold nucleus (79e). How close does it get?

topics.title: X-rays and Moseley's law
topics.search: X-rays discovery Roentgen and Moseley's law
topics.goal: X-ray lines order the elements by atomic number.
checks: I can use Moseley's rule E ≈ 10.2 eV × (Z − 1)².

ex.q: Predict the Kα X-ray energy of copper (Z = 29). The measured value is 8.05 keV.
Why did Moseley's work show that atomic number, not mass, orders the periodic table?
ex.a: The energies climbed smoothly with Z, not with mass

ex.q: Moseley found gaps that predicted missing elements. Which atomic numbers were they?

topics.title: Why classical atoms should collapse
topics.goal: Classical theory says orbiting electrons radiate and crash in about 10⁻¹¹ s.
checks: I can explain the classical prediction and why it failed.

ex.q: Classical physics predicts an orbiting electron spirals in within about 10⁻¹¹ s. Using 11.26, explain why it radiates at all.
ex.a: It is accelerating around its orbit

ex.q: As it spirals, its orbit frequency rises. What kind of spectrum would atoms then emit?

topics.title: The ultraviolet catastrophe
topics.goal: Classical physics predicts infinite energy at short wavelengths.
checks: I can explain why classical physics predicts infinite radiation.

ex.q: The Rayleigh-Jeans law grows as T/λ⁴. What happens at short wavelengths?
Why does counting modes in a box give more modes at higher frequency?
Why doesn't your oven blind you with ultraviolet?
ex.a: High-frequency modes need a whole quantum, which is rarely available.

topics.title: Rayleigh-Jeans versus Planck
topics.goal: Where the classical curve agrees with experiment and where it blows up.
checks: I can show where the classical and quantum laws agree.

ex.q: Show that Planck's law becomes Rayleigh-Jeans when hf ≪ kT.
The two differ by a factor of 2 when hf/kT ≈ 1.6. At 5800 K (kT ≈ 0.5 eV), at what wavelength is that?

topics.title: Planck's constant
topics.search: Planck's constant and quantization E = hf
topics.goal: Planck's fix: energy comes in packets hf.
checks: I can compute photon energies and photon counts.

ex.q: Find the energy of a 500 nm photon in joules.
How many photons per second does a 1 mW green laser emit?
Why does light look continuous to us?

topics.title: The photoelectric effect
topics.goal: Light knocks out electrons in packets (photons), set by frequency not brightness.
checks: I can use KE_max = hf − φ.

ex.q: Sodium's work function is 2.28 eV. Find its threshold wavelength.
400 nm light hits sodium. Find the maximum electron energy.
Why doesn't very bright red light eject any electrons?
ex.a: Each photon has too little energy

ex.q: What stopping voltage halts the electrons in Exercise 2?

topics.title: The hydrogen spectrum
topics.search: hydrogen spectrum Balmer series Rydberg formula
topics.goal: Hydrogen emits only specific wavelengths.
checks: I can use the Rydberg formula.

ex.q: Use 1/λ = R(1/4 − 1/n²) with R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ to find the n = 3 Balmer line.
Find the shortest Balmer wavelength (n → ∞).
Find the Lyman-α line (n = 2 → 1). Why can't you see it?

topics.title: The Bohr model
topics.goal: Quantized orbits explain hydrogen's lines (and where the model fails).
checks: I can derive Bohr's energies from L = nħ.

ex.q: Derive rₙ = n²a₀ and Eₙ = −13.6 eV/n² from L = nħ and circular motion.
Find the 3 → 2 photon energy and wavelength. Compare with 14.8.
Name three things the Bohr model cannot explain.

topics.title: The Franck-Hertz experiment
topics.goal: Atoms absorb energy only in fixed amounts.
checks: I can explain the dips in the current.

ex.q: Current drops every 4.9 V in mercury vapour. Why?
The excited mercury emits UV. Predict its wavelength.
Why was this direct proof of discrete energy levels?

topics.title: Compton scattering
topics.goal: Photons carry momentum like particles.
checks: I can use Δλ = (h/mc)(1 − cos θ).

ex.q: Find the largest possible wavelength shift (h/mc = 2.43 pm).
Why is the shift unnoticeable for visible light?
ex.a: Visible wavelengths are hundreds of nanometres

ex.q: Why does this prove photons carry momentum?
ex.a: Its shift follows from momentum conservation.

topics.title: Matter waves
topics.goal: Everything has a wavelength λ = h/p.
checks: I can compute de Broglie wavelengths.

ex.q: Find the wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V (λ ≈ 1.226/√V nm).
Find the wavelength of a 0.15 kg ball at 40 m/s.
Find it for a C₆₀ molecule (1.2 × 10⁻²⁴ kg) at 200 m/s. (See 23.24.)

topics.title: Electron diffraction
topics.goal: Electrons diffract like waves.
checks: I can predict where diffracted electrons appear.

ex.q: Davisson and Germer fired 54 eV electrons at nickel with atomic rows 0.215 nm apart. Predict the angle of the first peak from d sin θ = λ. (They saw 50°.)
Why do electron microscopes see far smaller things than light microscopes?

topics.title: The Stern-Gerlach experiment
topics.goal: Silver atoms split into exactly two beams: spin is quantized.
checks: I can explain the two spots and what they prove.

ex.q: What would classical physics predict on the screen?
Why do silver atoms work well? (Count their unpaired electrons.)
Silver's outer electron has no orbital angular momentum. What, then, splits the beam?

topics.title: The Zeeman effect
topics.goal: Spectral lines split in a magnetic field.
checks: I can estimate the size of Zeeman splittings.

ex.q: A 1 T field splits a level by about one Bohr magneton (58 μeV). How far does a 500 nm line shift?
How do astronomers use this to measure magnetic fields on the Sun?
ex.a: From the splitting of spectral lines in sunspots.

topics.title: The old quantum theory
topics.goal: The first quantization rules and why they were abandoned.
checks: I can apply Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization.

ex.q: Apply ∮ p dx = nh to a particle in a box of length L. Compare with the true answer (15.12).
Apply it to the oscillator (8.45). What is missing?
Why did the old theory fail for helium?
ex.a: Interacting electrons have no simple closed orbits.

topics.title: Young's original experiment
topics.goal: Thomas Young's experiment and its quantum future.
checks: I can explain what Young's experiment settled in 1801.

ex.q: What did Young's fringes prove about light?
Why had Newton preferred particles of light?

topics.title: Heisenberg on Helgoland
topics.goal: How Heisenberg invented quantum mechanics in 1925.
checks: I can tell the story of matrix mechanics.

ex.q: Why did Heisenberg build his theory only from observable quantities?
What did Born recognize in Heisenberg's tables, and why did xp ≠ px matter?
ex.a: They were matrices, and matrices need not commute.

topics.title: Schrödinger's wave mechanics
topics.goal: How the wave equation arrived.
checks: I can explain how wave mechanics arrived and how ψ was reinterpreted.

ex.q: What did Schrödinger first think ψ described? Why did Born's probability interpretation replace it?
ex.a: A smeared charge density; it did not fit how particles hit screens

ex.q: Who showed wave and matrix mechanics are the same theory?

topics.title: The Einstein-Bohr debates
topics.goal: The founders' arguments over what it all means.
checks: I can summarize their arguments.

ex.q: What did Einstein mean by "God does not play dice"?
Describe Einstein's photon-box challenge and how Bohr used Einstein's own gravity theory to answer it.
ex.a: Weighing the box shifts its clock by gravitational time dilation, restoring the uncertainty.

topics.title: Predicting antimatter
topics.search: Dirac antimatter prediction Anderson positron discovery
topics.goal: Theory predicted antimatter before it was seen.
checks: I can explain how the positron was predicted and found.

ex.q: How did Anderson's cloud chamber photo show a positive particle with the electron's mass?
ex.a: Its track curved the wrong way for an electron

ex.q: What is the least energy needed to create an electron-positron pair?

topics.title: The whole history
topics.goal: The whole story in one sitting.
checks: I can place the key discoveries on a timeline.

ex.q: Order these: Bohr model, Planck's quantum, positron, Schrödinger equation, photoelectric explanation, matrix mechanics, nucleus, matter waves, electron diffraction, Dirac equation.
ex.a: Planck 1900, photoelectric 1905, nucleus 1911, Bohr 1913, matter waves 1924, matrix mechanics 1925, Schrödinger 1926, electron diffraction 1927, Dirac 1928, positron 1932.

parts.name: QM Concepts
parts.title: Quantum mechanics, the concepts
parts.intro: Use ħ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and the handy fact that an electron in a 1 nm box has E₁ = 0.376 eV. Highlight: in 15.9 you show that if the electron really spun, its surface would move about 70 times faster than light.

topics.title: The double slit with single electrons
topics.goal: One particle at a time still builds an interference pattern.
checks: I can describe what builds up on the screen one electron at a time.

ex.q: Electrons are sent one at a time. What does the screen look like after 10 hits, after 10,000?
Add a detector that tells which slit each electron used. What happens to the pattern?
Where on the screen can an electron never land, and why?
ex.a: At the dark fringes, where the paths cancel.

topics.title: Wave-particle duality
topics.goal: Quantum objects are neither classical waves nor classical particles.
checks: I can name experiments that show each side of light and matter.

ex.q: Give one experiment showing light acts as a wave and one showing it acts as particles.
Do the same for electrons.
ex.a: Electron diffraction; individual hits on a screen.

ex.q: Is it right to say an electron "is" a wave? Argue both sides in two sentences each.

topics.title: The wavefunction
topics.goal: ψ(x) is a complex amplitude spread over space.
checks: I can sketch ψ and |ψ|² and explain why ψ can be complex.

ex.q: What does |ψ|² look like for ψ = A e^(ikx)?
Can ψ be negative or complex? Can |ψ|²?
ex.a: Yes; no, it is always real and non-negative.

ex.q: Sketch ψ and |ψ|² for ψ = sin(πx) and ψ = sin(2πx) on [0, 1].

topics.title: The Born rule
topics.goal: Probability density = ∣ψ∣²; amplitudes interfere, probabilities do not.
checks: I can turn amplitudes into probabilities.

ex.q: A state has amplitude 0.6 to be at A and 0.8i to be at B. Find both probabilities.
Redo 1.43 Exercise 1 and say which case is bright, dark and half.
Why must all probabilities add to 1?

topics.title: Normalizing a wavefunction
topics.goal: Scale ψ so the total probability is exactly 1.
checks: I can find the normalization constant for any simple ψ.

ex.q: ψ = A on [0, L], zero elsewhere.
ψ = A x(L − x) on [0, L].

topics.title: Superposition
topics.goal: A state can be a sum of other states.
checks: I can read measurement probabilities from a superposition.

ex.q: ψ = (ψ₁ + ψ₂)/√2. What is the chance of finding state 1?
ψ = (√3 ψ₁ + ψ₂)/2. Find both probabilities.
Is a 50/50 superposition the same as a box that is 50% one thing and 50% the other? (See 16.25.)

topics.title: Two-state systems
topics.goal: The simplest quantum system: two basis states and their superpositions.
checks: I can handle photon polarization as the simplest quantum system.

ex.q: A photon is diagonal, D = (H + V)/√2. What is the chance it passes a horizontal polarizer?
A photon is cos θ H + sin θ V. What is the chance it passes a polarizer at angle φ? Compare with 9.24.
Spin up along x is (↑ + ↓)/√2 in the z basis. What is the chance of measuring up along z?

topics.title: Measurement and collapse
topics.goal: Measuring gives one definite outcome and resets the state.
checks: I can predict what repeated measurements give.

ex.q: You measure spin up along z, then measure z again. What do you get?
Next you measure along x. What are the odds?
Then measure z again. What are the odds now? What did the x measurement do?
ex.a: 50/50: the x measurement erased the z information.

topics.title: The uncertainty principle
topics.goal: Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2 comes from wave behaviour, not clumsy measurement.
checks: I can use ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2 to estimate energies and sizes.

ex.q: An electron is confined to 0.1 nm. Estimate its minimum momentum spread and the kinetic energy that implies, in eV. Compare with atomic energies.
ex.a: About 5.3 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s; about 1 eV, the scale of atomic energies

ex.q: Could an electron live inside a nucleus 10⁻¹⁴ m wide? Estimate pc in MeV.
ex.a: pc ≈ 10 MeV, far more than nuclei offer electrons

ex.q: A 1 μg dust grain is located to 1 μm. What is its minimum velocity uncertainty?

topics.title: The Heisenberg microscope
topics.goal: Heisenberg's original argument and why it is not the full story.
checks: I can give Heisenberg's argument and say why it is incomplete.

ex.q: To see an electron with light of wavelength λ, you blur its position by about λ and kick it by about h/λ. Multiply them.
Why does uncertainty exist even if nobody measures anything?
ex.a: It is a property of the state, not of clumsy measuring.

ex.q: Look up Ozawa's error-disturbance relation and the 2012 neutron experiment that tested it.

topics.title: Energy-time uncertainty
topics.goal: Short-lived states have spread-out energies (line widths).
checks: I can link lifetimes to energy spreads.

ex.q: An excited atom lives 10 ns. Estimate its energy spread in eV and its line width in MHz.
The Z boson's mass peak is 2.5 GeV wide. Estimate its lifetime.
Why is energy-time uncertainty different from position-momentum uncertainty?
ex.a: Time is a parameter, not an observable.

topics.title: Quantization
topics.goal: Bound systems allow only certain energies.
checks: I can explain why confined waves have discrete energies.

ex.q: How is a guitar string's set of notes like an atom's set of energies? (See 5.8.)
Is a free electron's energy quantized?
What sets how far apart the levels are?
ex.a: The size of the confinement and the mass.

topics.title: Spin
topics.goal: Spin is intrinsic angular momentum, not literal spinning.
checks: I can state spin values and explain why spin is not literal rotation.

ex.q: What values can S_z take for an electron?
How many values can S_z take for a spin-1 particle?
Suppose the electron were a ball of radius 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ m carrying angular momentum ħ/2. How fast would its equator move? Compare with c.
ex.a: About 2 × 10¹⁰ m/s, about 70c: so it is not literally spinning.

topics.title: The Schrödinger equation
topics.goal: How the equation evolves ψ in time.
checks: I can write the equation and check simple solutions.

ex.q: Check that e^(i(kx − ωt)) solves the free equation if ω = ħk²/(2m).
Why does linearity guarantee superposition works?
The heat equation (5.9) looks similar but has no i. What does the i change?

topics.title: Stationary states
topics.goal: Energy eigenstates only change by a phase.
checks: I can separate time and show |ψ|² is constant for energy eigenstates.

ex.q: Put ψ = φ(x) e^(−iEt/ħ) into the Schrödinger equation. What equation does φ satisfy?
Show |ψ|² does not change in time.
Why are these called stationary states?

topics.title: Superpositions in time
topics.search: superposition of energy eigenstates time evolution quantum beats
topics.goal: Superpositions of different energies slosh back and forth in time.
checks: I can show a superposition of energies sloshes back and forth.

ex.q: Show that |ψ|² for (φ₁e^(−iE₁t/ħ) + φ₂e^(−iE₂t/ħ))/√2 oscillates at frequency (E₂ − E₁)/h.
For an electron in a 1 nm box, find that frequency for levels 1 and 2.
What frequency of light would the electron emit dropping from 2 to 1? Compare.

topics.title: The particle in a box
topics.search: particle in a box infinite square well
topics.goal: Derive Eₙ ∝ n²; draw the wavefunctions.
checks: I can derive the energies and draw the wavefunctions.

ex.q: Derive Eₙ = n²π²ħ²/(2mL²) using 5.8.
For an electron in a 1 nm box, list E₁, E₂ and E₃.
Find the photon wavelength for the 2 → 1 jump.
In the ground state, what is the chance of finding the particle in the middle third?
What happens to the probability density at very large n? Why does this match classical physics?
ex.a: It becomes uniform, like a ball bouncing back and forth.

topics.title: The finite square well
topics.goal: A finite well has a limited number of bound states, and ψ leaks into the walls.
checks: I can explain bound states and wavefunction leakage.

ex.q: Why does a 1D finite well always have at least one bound state?
ex.a: Any attractive 1D well holds a state

ex.q: An electron is 1 eV below the rim. Find the decay length 1/κ of its wavefunction outside, with κ = √(2m(V − E))/ħ.
Why are the energies lower than in an infinite well of the same width?
ex.a: The wavefunction spreads into the walls.

topics.title: Quantum tunneling
topics.goal: Particles cross barriers they classically cannot (the decay is exponential in width).
checks: I can estimate tunneling probabilities with T ≈ e^(−2κa).

ex.q: An electron faces a barrier 1 eV above its energy and 1 nm wide. Estimate T.
Double the width. What happens to T?
Explain in one sentence why you will never tunnel through a wall.
ex.a: The mass and width make 2κa astronomically large

ex.q: In a scanning tunneling microscope the barrier is about 4 eV. By what factor does the current change when the tip moves 0.1 nm?

topics.title: Reflection from a step
topics.goal: Particles can reflect even when they have enough energy to pass.
checks: I can compute quantum reflection at a step.

ex.q: A particle with E = 2V₀ meets a step of height V₀. Find R = ((k₁ − k₂)/(k₁ + k₂))².
What would classical physics predict?
Does a particle also reflect when stepping down? Check with the formula.
ex.a: Yes: the formula is symmetric in k₁ and k₂.

topics.title: The quantum harmonic oscillator
topics.goal: Equally spaced levels Eₙ = ħω(n + ½).
checks: I can use Eₙ = ħω(n + ½).

ex.q: How far apart are neighbouring levels?
CO vibrates at 2143 cm⁻¹ (1 cm⁻¹ = 1.24 × 10⁻⁴ eV). Find ħω in eV.
Why are oscillator levels evenly spaced while box levels grow as n²?

topics.title: Zero-point energy
topics.goal: The lowest energy is never zero.
checks: I can explain why the ground state is never at rest.

ex.q: Find CO's zero-point energy.
Use the uncertainty principle to explain why E₀ cannot be 0.
ex.a: Sitting still at the bottom would mean Δx = Δp = 0

ex.q: Which two strange effects in this roadmap come from zero-point energy? (See 10.4 and 23.1.)
ex.a: Liquid helium and the Casimir effect.

topics.title: Wave packets spread
topics.goal: Localized particles spread over time.
checks: I can estimate how fast a free particle's wave packet spreads.

ex.q: A Gaussian spreads as σ(t) = σ₀√(1 + (ħt/(2mσ₀²))²). How long until an electron localized to 0.1 nm doubles in width?
Do the same for a 1 g marble localized to 1 μm.
ex.a: About 3 × 10¹⁹ s, far longer than the age of the universe

ex.q: Which property of waves (9.27) causes the spreading?

topics.title: Expectation values
topics.goal: Compute average position and momentum from ψ.
checks: I can compute ⟨x⟩, ⟨x²⟩ and Δx.

ex.q: Find ⟨x⟩ for the box ground state.
Why is ⟨p⟩ = 0 for any real wavefunction?
ex.a: ⟨p⟩ = −iħ∫ψψ′ dx is purely imaginary for real ψ but must be real, so it is 0

ex.q: Find Δx for the box ground state, given ⟨x²⟩ = L²(1/3 − 1/(2π²)).

topics.title: Probability current
topics.goal: How probability flows.
checks: I can compute how probability flows.

ex.q: Find the current J = (ħ/m) Im(ψ* dψ/dx) for ψ = A e^(ikx).
Show any real wavefunction has zero current.
Write the continuity equation for probability (compare 4.17).

topics.title: The delta-function well
topics.goal: The simplest bound state and scattering problem.
checks: I can solve the simplest bound state.

ex.q: For V = −αδ(x), show the bound state is ψ = √κ e^(−κ|x|) and find κ from the jump in slope.
Find the bound-state energy.

topics.title: Quantum mechanics in 3D
topics.search: quantum mechanics in 3D separation of variables
topics.goal: Boxes and oscillators in 3D; degeneracy.
checks: I can find energies and degeneracies in a cubic box.

ex.q: In a cube, E ∝ nₓ² + n_y² + n_z². List the first five values and their degeneracies.
Why does the cube's symmetry cause degeneracy?
The 3D oscillator level n has (n + 1)(n + 2)/2 states. Check it for n = 0, 1, 2.

topics.title: The Mach-Zehnder interferometer
topics.goal: The cleanest experiment for superposition and interference.
checks: I can track single photons through an interferometer.

ex.q: In a balanced interferometer every photon leaves one port. Why?
ex.a: The two paths cancel at the other port

ex.q: Block one arm. What fraction reach each detector now?
ex.a: Half are absorbed; a quarter reach each detector

ex.q: Why does blocking a path you didn't take change where you go? (See 19.20.)
ex.a: Because the photon's amplitude travelled both arms.

topics.title: Entanglement
topics.goal: Joint states that cannot be split into separate parts.
checks: I can describe entangled measurement results and why they don't send messages.

ex.q: For (↑↓ − ↓↑)/√2, you measure the first spin up. What is the second?
Show this state is not a product state (3.27).
Why can't Alice use entanglement to send Bob a message?
ex.a: Each side alone sees random results.

topics.title: The EPR paradox
topics.goal: Einstein's argument that quantum mechanics is incomplete.
checks: I can state the EPR argument.

ex.q: Summarize EPR's argument in three sentences.
What did they mean by an "element of reality"?
ex.a: A value you can predict with certainty without disturbing the system.

topics.title: Bell's theorem
topics.search: Bell's theorem quantum Venn diagram paradox
topics.goal: Correlations no local hidden variables can explain.
checks: I can show quantum correlations break a Bell-type inequality.

ex.q: Entangled photons disagree with probability sin²(angle difference). Polarizers sit at 0°, 22.5° and 45°. Local hidden variables require P(0, 45) ≤ P(0, 22.5) + P(22.5, 45). Check whether quantum mechanics obeys it.
ex.a: sin² 45° = 0.5 but sin² 22.5° + sin² 22.5° ≈ 0.29: it fails

ex.q: What does the violation rule out?

topics.title: Schrödinger's cat
topics.goal: Superposition scaled up to absurdity.
checks: I can explain what the cat was meant to show.

ex.q: Was Schrödinger promoting the idea of a dead-and-alive cat?
ex.a: No: he meant it as an absurdity

ex.q: Why do we never see cats in superposition? (See 15.30.)

topics.title: The quantum eraser
topics.goal: Which-path information destroys interference (and what it does not prove).
checks: I can explain why erasing which-path information brings fringes back only in sorted data.

ex.q: Mark the two slits with different polarizations. What happens to the fringes, and why?
ex.a: They vanish: the paths are distinguishable

ex.q: Why can't the eraser send messages into the past?
ex.a: The raw pattern never shows fringes.

topics.title: Wheeler's delayed choice
topics.goal: The choice of measurement made after the photon passes.
checks: I can explain the experiment without retrocausality.

ex.q: Describe the experiment in your own words.
